OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2025-26) OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF SCHOOL EDUCATION & LITERACY (DoSE&L) 
Recommendation  
1. The Committee observes that there is 6.9% increase in BE allocation 2025-26 vis-à-vis BE 
allocation 2024-25 while there was an increase of 8.44% in BE 2023-24 vis-à-vis BE allocation 
2022-23 for Department of School Education and Literacy. The Committee feels that in view of 
the inflationary trends in the country, the allocation should increase at least 8% to 10% over the 
allocation during previous year to accommodate the inflation and to maintain the existing 
standards for expenditure by Department of School Education and Literacy and to avoid decline 
in actual allocation/expenditure for school education. The current allocations are, therefore, 
disappointing – especially in the context of the need for adequate resources to implement the 
NEP. 
(Para 2.4 ibid) 
2. From analysis of the Table 3,4 and 5 given above, the Committee observes that there is 
6.90 % increase in BE 2025-56 in comparison to BE 2024-25 and 16.28% increase over RE 2024-
25. The Committee further observes that there is an increase of 8.44% in BE 2023-24 vis-à-vis BE 
2022-23. The Department had made projections of Rs. 84,100.84 crores to the Ministry of 
Finance for 2025-26. However, the actual allocation to the Department is Rs. 78,572.1 crores 
which reflects the variation/decrease of -6.57 % between projections made to the Ministry of 
Finance and actual allocation made to Department of School Education and Literacy in BE 2025-
26. 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to undertake review of the 
Projections made to Ministry of Finance and actual allocations to the Department in respect of 
each scheme run by the Department wherein there is gap between Projections and allocations to 
make it realistic. The Committee also recommends the Department to monitor the physical and 
financial progress of the schemes, so that, these schemes do not suffer due to reduced allocations. 
Such an objective review will help the Department to seek additional funds at RE stage for the 
schemes being run. 
(Para 2.6 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 For the Department of School Education and Literacy, the Budget Allocation for the FY 
2025-26 of ₹ 78572 Cr is the highest ever for the Department of School Education & Literacy. 
The highlights of the Budget allocation are: - 
 There has been an overall increase of ₹ 5074 Cr (7%) in the Budget Allocation of 
Department of School Education and Literacy in the FY 2025-26 from BE 2024-25. As 
compared to RE of FY 2024-25, there has been an increase of ₹ 11,000 Cr (16.28%). 
 The highest ever Budget Allocation may be seen in the Autonomous Body of Kendriya 
Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS) at Rs. 9,503 Cr. Allocation in KVS has increased by ₹ 201.17 
Cr as compared to Budget allocation of FY 2024-25. There has been an increase of ₹ 776 
Cr (9%) as compared to RE of FY 2024-25. 

3 
 
 Budget Allocation of FY 2025-26 in Flagship Schemes have increased i.e Samagra 
Shiksha (by ₹ 3750 Cr), PM-POSHAN (by ₹ 32 Cr) and PM-SHRI (by ₹ 1450 Cr) with 
respect to Budget Allocation (BE) of FY 2024-25. As compared to RE 2024-25, allocation 
in Samagra Shiksha has increased by ₹ 4240 Cr (11%), allocation in PM-POSHAN has 
increased by ₹ 2500 Cr (25 %) and allocation in PM-SHRI has increased by ₹ 3000 Cr 
(66%). 
 Out of the overall Budget Allocation in FY 2025-26 of ₹ 78,572 Cr, the Scheme allocation 
is ₹ 63,089 Cr and Non-Scheme Allocation is ₹ 15,483 Cr. 
 Increase in Scheme Allocation in BE 2025-26 is ₹ 5284 Cr (9.14 %) as compared to BE 
2024-25. As compared to RE 24-25, increase in Scheme Allocation is ₹ 10248 Cr (19%) 
and non-Scheme allocation has increased by ₹ 752 Cr (5%) in BE 2025-26. 
Further, Economic Survey 2024-25 notes that there is a rising trend in Government’s social 
services expenditure (SSE), as a percentage of total expenditure (TE).  While the SSE outlay of 
the Centre and State governments was Rs. 14.8 lakh crore in FY21, it has increased steadily to 
stand at ₹25.7 lakh crore in FY25 (BE). 
On Education, the Survey notes that the expenditure in the sector has grown at a CAGR of 12%, 
from Rs. 5.8 lakh crore in FY21 to Rs. 9.2 lakh crore in FY25 (BE).  
Budget proposals of the Department projected to the MoF are finalized only after due 
deliberations. Further, the physical & financial progress of the Schemes are continually monitored

Recommendation  
3. From figures given at Table 8, it is evident that Rs. 73,498.1 crores has been allocated 
under BE 2024-25 which has been decreased to Rs.67,571.2 crores at RE stage. The Committee 
observes that this reduction at RE stage amounts to Rs.5,926.9 crores which is 8.06% less in 
comparison to allocation at BE 2024-25. Further, the Committee notes that the Actual 
expenditure of the Department is only Rs. 43,254.81 crores as on 18.02.2025 which is 64.01% of 
the reduced allocations of RE 2024-25. In this regard, the Committee would like to refer to Rule 
56(3) of General Financial Rules (GFR), which states that rush to expenditure particularly in the 
closing months of financial year shall be regarded as a breach of financial propriety and shall be 
avoided. As per the guidelines, the last quarter expenditure must be limited to actual procurement 
of goods and services and reimbursement of expenditure already occurred. Ministry of Finance's 
instructions seeks to restrict last quarter expenditure to 33% ceiling and last month (March) 
expenditure to 15% ceiling only. 
 
In backdrop of the Actual Expenditure by Department of School Education and Literacy 
during 2024-25 and Rule 56(3) of General Financial Rules (GFR), the Committee recommends 
that the Department should adhere to Rule 56(3) of GFR, streamline its expenditure during 2025-
26 to optimize the utilization of funds allocated to it and to avoid piling up of expenditure in the 
last quarter of the financial year. 
(Para 2.12ibid) 
Action Taken 
During the financial year 2024-25 the actual expenditure incurred by the Department was 
Rs. 64519.64 crores which represents over 95% expenditure against the RE of Rs. 67571.20 
crores.

Recommendation  
5. The Committee observes that resource allocation is grossly insufficient. Out of Rs. 41,250 
crores allocated to Samagra Shiksha, Rs. 35,000 crore goes to primary education. Only the 
remaining Rs 6,250 crore is for secondary education. This lopsided allocation raises questions on 
the Department’s seriousness in reaching the NEP’s stated goals of universal secondary 
education by 2030.Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Department should 
significantly enhance the budget of the SSA and reserve these funds for the enhancement of 
secondary schools. 
(Para 3.3ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
Under Samagra Shiksha, all States and UTs submit their proposals for all interventions 
contained in the scheme through their Annual Work Plan & Budget (AWP&B). The proposals are 
appraised and approved by the Project Approval Board (PAB) as per the programmatic and 
financial norms of Samagra Shiksha in the Ministry, in consultation with the respective State/UT 
government and proportionate funds are allocated.  The funds, under the scheme of Samagra 
Shiksha, are released based on the fulfilment of guidelines prescribed by Ministry of Finance, 
such as transfer of central share to SNA, pace of expenditure, receipt of commensurate State share 
in SNA, statement on outstanding advances, up-to date expenditure statement, furnishing of 
information as prescribed in the Manual on Financial Management & Procurement and audited 
utilization certificate of previous year. 
In FY 2018-19, Rs. 3400.24 Crore was released as Central Share under Secondary 
Education while in 2024-25 it was 5971.28 Crore which is an increase of more than 75%. During 
annual PAB meetings with the States/UTs, they are sensitized for enhancing their allocation in 
Secondary education scheme of Samagra Shiksha. During the in-person meeting held on 17th 
January 2025 with States and UTs, they were guided to enhance allocation for secondary 
education also as per requirement. 
The Department is taking steps to ensure allocations are in a proportionate and focused 
manner. In the current year Rs. 5989 Crores has been allocated vide a supplementary PAB for 
saturating ICT, Smart Classes and Physics/Chemistry/Biology laboratories in secondary / Hr 
secondary schools, in addition to the regular allocation.                                         
 
SAMAGRA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN (SSA) 
Recommendation  
6. The goal of the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan is to enable RTE implementation in state 
schools. However, the Committee is pained to note that 15 years after the RTE Act was passed, we 
have still not reached universal achievement of RTE norms by schools and teachers. In far too 
many schools, the pupil-teacher ratio, the number of classrooms, or the availability of water and 

6 
 
sanitation facilities and/or playgrounds is inadequate. The Committee notes the tremendous 
achievements of the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan but calls for a revamping of the scheme to function 
on mission mode. The mission must be to achieve near-saturation of the RTE’s requirements by 
2029. The Finance Minister’s Budget announcement of achieving universal broadband 
connectivity for rural secondary schools within the year offers a model for the scale and timeline 
at which the Government should be operating at to upgrade the physical and human resources 
offered by schools. 
At the same time, it is not advisable to impose the RTE’s norms and requirements on 
schools without fore thought. There are several schools, especially in underserved, remote, and 
Adivasi-majority areas, which may be unable to meet the formal requirements demanded by the 
RTE. Recently, the only Gondi-language school in Maharashtra, in Gadchiroli district, was 
forced to shut down since it did not have the requisite approval from the State Government as 
mandated by the RTE. Similar stories have emerged from ST dominant areas in Assam. 
Recognizing that the only feasible alternative to these schools is no school, the Department must 
relax RTE norms in such instances. Relaxation of RTE norms can only be done with a view to 
preserve schools – not with a view to consolidate them or to continue to under-resource them. 
(Para 3.4.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
Education is in the concurrent list of the Constitution and an overwhelming majority of the 
schools are under the jurisdiction of the concerned States & UTs. State and UT Governments 
are the appropriate Governments under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory 
Education (RTE) Act, 2009, and have the responsibility and mandate to provide school 
infrastructure in schools in accordance with the norms laid down in the Schedule to the RTE 
Act, 2009 and as per respective State RTE Rules. 
  However, under Samagra Shiksha, States and UTs are supported for strengthening of 
existing government schools and for creation and augmentation of infrastructure facilities, 
based on the gaps determined from Unified District Information System for Education 
(UDISE) database and proposals received from respective State/UT. The requirement of 
infrastructural facilities in schools are worked out every year by the respective State/Union 
Territory on incremental basis depending on their need and priority and reflected in their 
Annual Work Plan and Budget (AWP&B). The budget plans are appraised/approved by PAB 
in consultation with the States and UTs as per the programmatic and financial norms of the 
Scheme and availability of budgetary resources. 
  DoSE&L is taking steps for saturation in providing Infrastructure facilities to the 
States. In this regard, the States/UTs have been requested in various forums including the 
meeting of the Project Approval Board, review meetings and other forums for filling up the 
gaps in school infrastructure.  
  In pursuance to other Para of 363rd Report of DRPSC, this Department has issued various 
advisory/guidelines in this regard to the States/UTs.  DO letter dated 03.07.2025 to all States/ 
UTs advising them to identify gaps in provision of safe and potable drinking water through 
taps and separate Girls’ toilets in all Govt/ Govt. Aided schools. 
  
Further, in convergence with DDWS and MoHUA this Department is enabling provisioning 
of safe and potable drinking water through taps and separate Girls’ toilets through their 
Schemes.

At the State/UT level, consolidation, opening and closure of schools is under State/UT

Samagra Shiksha norms underline that consolidation/merger of school shall not in any 
case violate the right of access to school of a single child as per neighbourhood norms notified by 
the respective State/UT under the RTE Act 2009.

Recommendation  
9. The Committee notes that in some areas, considerable number of the children in schools 
that have shut down drop out of the school, and that the effects are disproportionately felt by girl 
children, children with disabilities, and Scheduled Tribe and Scheduled Caste communities. In 
this context, the Committee feels that being the nodal Department for school education, it is 
responsibility of the Department to collect data on school closures and consolidations and 
Committee should be apprised thereof. The lack of data precludes any systematic study or policy 
of the impact that such school closures may have on students.  The Committee, therefore, directs 
the Department to develop a policy on school closure and consolidation. Some features of such a 
policy may include – 
 Clear guidelines on when it is acceptable to consider school consolidation, ensuring that 
RTE guidelines are not violated 
 Mandatory impact assessment of each school closure

The Committee also feels that any school consolidations or closures should not violate RTE 
norms on the physical proximity of primary schools to children. The Committee notes that in its 
discussion of school complexes, the NEP does not reiterate the RTE’s guidance on the necessity to 
have primary schools (Grade I-V) within 1 km of a neighborhood and upper primary schools 
(Grade VI-VIII) within 3 km of a neighborhood. However, this does not mean that the NEP’s 
proposed school complexes overrule or modify the provisions of the RTE Act, 2009. The 
Committee emphasizes that the RTE is a law passed by Parliament which deals with the 
fundamental rights of Indian children and. Department should evolve a mechanism to ensure that

The School Education System in Bharat is one of the largest in the world with more than 
14.72 lakh schools, more than 98 lakh teachers and around 24.80 Crore students from pre-primary 
to higher secondary level from varied socio-economic backgrounds. Among the schools, there are 
69.14% government schools, 22.5% private schools, 5.5% aided schools, and 2.86% other 
schools. The school system has ten different school categories running in parallel. 
As per UDISE+ 2023-24, the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) across different levels of 
school Education are: Foundational stage - 77.7%; Preparatory stage – 96.5%; Middle stage – 
89.5%; and Secondary stage – 66.5%.  Further, as per UDISE+ (2023-24), the dropout rate at the 
Foundational, Preparatory and Secondary stage is 3.7%. 5.2% and 10.9%, respectively.  
The current policy imperative is to realize the NEP 2020's objective of attaining a 100% 
GER from pre-school through secondary levels by 2030. The Gender Parity Index shows equal 
participation of both boys and girls across all levels of school education i.e., Foundational – 1.00; 
Preparatory – 1.03; Middle – 1.02; and Secondary – 1.04.  
As per UDISE 2023-24, there are 12954 schools with zero enrolment and 31981 teachers 
in schools having zero enrolment. These result in underutilized resources. To achieve better 
learning outcomes with at least two teachers per school and appropriate Pupil-Teacher Ratios 
(PTR) across upper primary and secondary levels, some states have adopted appropriate strategies 
to establish the larger schools as per the aspirations of the public. 
Under the centrally sponsored scheme of Samagra Shiksha, various provisions are 
provided, including provision for transport and escort facility up to the secondary level for 
children in remote habitations with sparse population where opening of schools is unviable or 
where Gross Access Ratio is low  and where schools are not available within the prescribed area 
or setting up of a new school is not feasible and there is no State scheme for supporting transport 
facility. For FY2025-26, a total amount of Rs. 453.56 crore has been approved for covering 
10,70,707 children. 
The decline in schools over 2021-22 & 2022-23 is marginal.  On the other hand,

education. This is evidenced by a Gross Access Ratio (GAR- 2024-25) of 97.83% at Primary

Action Taken 
The Samagra Shiksha Scheme is aligned with the recommendations of the National 
Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and aims to ensure that all children have access to quality education 
with an equitable and inclusive classroom environment which should take care of their diverse 
background, multilingual needs, different academic abilities and make them active participants in 
the learning process. 
Framework for implementation of Samagra Shiksha has provisions of monitoring the 
progress including the quality of education at different level i.e. District level, State level and 
National level. Following mechanisms are being adopted to ensure quality education under 
Samagra Shiksha: 
 Performance Grading Index: The Performance Grading Index (PGI) has been designed to 
cater to the transformational change in the field of school education, where the focus has 
now shifted to the quality of education.  The index comprising of 73 indicators is propelling 
State and UTs towards undertaking multipronged interventions that will bring about the 
much desired educational outcomes.   
 UDISE+: This is an improved and updated version of Unified District Information System 
for Education (UDISE) for evidence-based planning and decision making. 
 Vidya Samiksha Kendra (VSK) - Vidya Samiksha Kendra (VSK) is aimed at leveraging data 
and technology to bring a bid leap in learning outcomes. This will cover data of schools, 
teachers and students to analyse them meaningfully using big data analysis, artificial 
intelligence and machine learning in order to enhance the overall monitoring of the education 
system and thereby improving learning outcomes. Support has been provided under Samagra 
Shiksha to set up VSK in all State and UTs.   
 National Achievement Surveys (NAS) now called PARAKH RashtriyaSarvekshan are 
conducted at regular intervals to check the health of the educational system and to provide 
information about the learning achievement of students.  
 Detailed guidelines for Social Audit of Samagra Shiksha have been issued and provision has 
been made for covering 20% government and government aided schools every year for 
conducting social audit. 
 Audit Mechanism- There are robust monitoring systems in place which includes an annual 
audit by an independent Chartered Accountant empanelled with the Comptroller and Auditor 
General (CAG) of India, a regular CAG audit, a system of concurrent financial reviews and 
regular meetings with State officials. A Manual on Financial Management and Procurement 
also assists States in streamlining implementation and financial management. 
 Periodic meetings with Stakeholders: The Ministry of Education convenes monthly meetings 
with Education Secretaries and State Project Directors to review the programme 
implementation.   
 Strengthening of Block Resource Centers and Cluster Resource Centers for periodic 
inspection and supervision of schools to observe the infrastructure and facilities  
 Community Level Monitoring- Monitoring under the programme is a three tiered one: 
monitoring at the local community level, at the State level and the National level. 
Community based monitoring is one of the strengths of the programme. The community, 
through its representative institutions like School Management Committees (SMCs), has 
been entrusted with the primary level of ensuring that the schools are functioning effectively. 
 NCERT is bringing out engaging textbooks to hold the attention of students and introduce 
them to experiential learning, in accordance with NCF-SE. 

17 
 
 Teachers are being trained to teach with better pedagogical skills. SCERTs and DIETs are 
being upgraded to Centres of Excellence. 
In pursuance of the recommendation of the NEP 2020, the National Assessment Centre, 
PARAKH (Performance Assessment, Review, and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic 
Development), was established on 8th February, 2023 by the Ministry of Education under the 
National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT). It serves as a central body for 
setting standards, conducting large-scale assessments, and providing evidence-based policy 
recommendations to improve the quality of education. Since its inception, PARAKH has 
undertaken the following activities with an aim to monitor the quality the education being 
imparted in schools and suggesting evidence based remedial measures: 
 
1. The PARAKH RashtriyaSarvekshan, which is a baseline study to understand the achievement 
of the stage specific competencies at the end of foundation, preparatory and middle stages as per 
NEP 2020, was conducted on 4.12.2024 in 781 districts of the country. The survey witnessed 
participation of 21,15,022 students and 2,70,424 teachers from 74,229 schools. The survey's data 
collection and analysis are aimed at strengthening accountability mechanisms, guiding future 
educational reforms and providing data-driven insights for policy interventions. 
2. Development of Holistic Progress Cards (HPC) - a competency-based assessment tool - which 
provides 360 degrees multidimensional holistic progress of learners across cognitive, affective, 
psychomotor and skill domains. Aligned with the curriculum structure as recommended by NEP 
2020, HPC spans across the foundational, preparatory, middle and secondary education stages. 
These progress cards help in identifying students’ unique abilities, strengths and areas for 
improvement, fostering a supportive learning environment. 
3. In an effort to standardize assessment practices, PARAKH has undertaken an empirical study to 
establish equivalence among different State education boards. The findings offer guidelines on 
critical aspects such as assessment, infrastructure, curriculum, inclusion and administration. 
Equivalence among difference boards will foster a level playing field for all students, enabling 
them to compete fairly in higher education admissions and job markets. 
4. PARAKH has also played a crucial role in advocating for the adoption of the State School 
Standards Authority (SSSA) and the School Quality Assessment and Accreditation Framework 
(SQAAF). The SSSA will establish a minimal set of standards based on basic parameters namely, 
safety, security, basic infrastructure, number of teachers across subjects and grades, financial 
probity, and sound processes of governance, which shall be followed by all schools. The 
framework for these parameters i.e. SQAAF, will be created in consultation with various 
stakeholders, especially teachers and schools. PARAKH has created a model SQAAF for 
adoption/adaption by States/UTs. 
5. PARAKH also implements an initiative namely “Udyam Sansaar” or World of Work (WoW), 
which complements the HPC framework. It promotes a multidisciplinary curriculum, skill-based 
learning, and exposure to emerging technologies like Artificial Intelligence, helping students 
develop competencies aligned with real-world needs. It reinforces the shift towards a competency-
based and inclusive education system, as envisioned in NEP 2020. 
Recommendation  
18. The Committee notes that GER at Elementary, Secondary and Higher Secondary levels 
have shown declining trends during 2023-24 in comparison to 2021-22 and 2022-23. It is also 

18 
 
worth mentioning that dropout rates at Primary, Upper Primary and Secondary levels are higher 
than that of 2021-22. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Department should strive for 
arresting the decline in GER ratio ensure 100% retention of students in the country. 
(Para 3.4.27ibid) 
Action Taken 
As per Para 3.1 of NEP 2020, one of the primary goals of the schooling system must be to ensure 
that children are enrolled in and are attending school. Accordingly, two overall initiatives will be 
undertaken to bring children who have dropped out back to school and to prevent further children 
from dropping out (para 3.2). The first is to provide effective and sufficient infrastructure so that 
all students have access to safe and engaging school education at all levels from pre-primary 
school to Grade 12. The second is to achieve universal participation in school by carefully 
tracking students, as well as their learning levels, in order to ensure that they (a) are enrolled in 
and attending school, and (b) have suitable opportunities to catch up and re-enter school in case 
they have fallen behind or dropped out.  
As per Para 3.4 of NEP, once infrastructure and participation are in place, ensuring quality 
will be the key in retention of students, so that they (particularly, girls and students from other 
socio-economically disadvantaged groups) do not lose interest in attending school. In keeping 
with this, financial provisions for various qualitative interventions are provided under Samagra 
Shiksha such as learning enhancement programme for children falling behind, teaching learning 
materials for children from pre-primary to class 5, assessment at the state and district level, 
holistic progress card, exposure to skill education, etc. 
States/UTs have been advised to take efforts to increase enrolment by taking certain steps 
like maintaining adequate PTR, improving transition rates etc. States also organize various 
Enrolment Drives and Awareness Campaigns, annually at the beginning of the academic session 
and also during the course of the year, to bring children back to school.  
Further, States/UTs are provided financial assistance under Samagra Shiksha to improve 
enrolment and retention in schools through interventions such as identification and mainstreaming 
of Out-of-School Children (OoSC), support  through NIOS/SIOS for OoSC for age group 16-19 
years, transport & escort facility for children in remote habitations, strengthening and upgradation 
of schools, provision of residential schools/hostels (NSCBAV, KGBV, PM-JANMAN, 
DAJGUA), strengthening Early Childhood and Foundational Learning, etc. 
Recommendation  
19. The Committee is of the view that the current policy framework to achieve the NEP’s goal 
of universal secondary education by 2030 is grossly insufficient. Apart from the mere existence of 
secondary schools, there is no rights-based entitlement, nationwide policy, and monitoring 
mechanism to ensure minimal drop-outs and 100% retention of students from primary to 
secondary school. Accordingly, to give teeth to the NEP’s vision of universal secondary 
education, the RTE must be amended to extend the right to education until the age of 18.A set of 
clear entitlements must be identified, a protocol must be put in place to prevent dropouts, and 
norms must be established on the setting up of secondary schools. 
(Para 3.4.28ibid) 

19 
 
Action Taken 
The Samagra Shiksha, aligned with NEP 2020, scheme aims to ensure that all children 
have access to quality education with an equitable and inclusive classroom environment which 
should take care of their diverse background, multilingual needs, different academic abilities and 
make them active participants in the learning process. 
To bring children who have dropped out back to school and to prevent further children 
from dropping out, National Education Policy (NEP 2020) suggests two overall initiatives. The 
first is to provide effective and sufficient infrastructure so that all students have access to safe and 
engaging school education at all levels from pre-primary school to Grade 12. Besides providing 
regular trained teachers at each stage, NEP suggests that special care shall be taken to ensure that 
no school remains deficient on infrastructure support. The credibility of Government schools shall 
be re-established and this will be attained by upgrading and enlarging the schools that already 
exist, building additional quality schools in areas where they do not exist, and providing safe and 
practical conveyances and/or hostels, especially for the girl children, so that all children have the 
opportunity to attend a quality school and learn at the appropriate level. Alternative and 
innovative education centres will be put in place in cooperation with civil society to ensure that 
children of migrant labourers, and other children who are dropping out of school due to various 
circumstances are brought back into mainstream education. 
The Samagra Shiksha scheme has also been aligned with the recommendations of NEP 
2020. Under the scheme, for providing universal access to quality secondary education, the 
neighbourhood norms notified by the state/UT would be applicable for opening of new secondary 
and senior secondary schools. In the case of States/UTs, which have not notified the 
neighbourhood norms for secondary and senior secondary Schools, the scheme will provide 
support for access to secondary school within a distance of 5 Km and senior secondary school 
within 7-10 Km of a habitation while ensuring their viability and cost effectiveness. 
The need for schools and also the infrastructural facilities in schools, to reduce drop out and 
ensure retention, are worked out every year by the respective State/Union Territory on 
incremental basis depending on their need and priority and reflected in their Annual Work plan & 
Budget (AWP&B). Financial assistance is also provided to States and UTS for undertaking 
various activities to ensure universal access to education including opening/strengthening of new

Action Taken 
CBSE has laid down specific provisions for determination of fees charged by schools.  
Chapter 7 of Affiliation Bye Laws of the Board stipulates that Societies /Trust /Companies are 
required to run schools in accordance with the provisions contained in these Bye Laws, “the 
School shall endeavour to charge fees to the extent the expenses for running the School are met. 
Schools shall follow the following norms in respect of the fees charged from pupils:”   
   No Society/Trust/Company/School shall charge capitation fee or accept donations for the 
purpose of admission for pupils. 
   Admission Fee and Fee charged under any other head are to be charged only as per the 
regulations of the Appropriate Government. 
   Fees shall be charged under the heads prescribed by the Department of Education of the 
State/UTs. 
   The acts and regulations of the Central and State/UT Governments enacted/framed in 
connection with regulation of fee in respect of the various categories of the schools situated in the 
state will be applicable to the school affiliated with CBSE also. 
   Fee revision of schools shall be subject to laws, regulation and directions of the Appropriate 
Government. 
   Fee shall not be revised without the express approval of the School Management Committee 
or the process prescribed by the Appropriate Government under any circumstances.

The Board vide Circular No. CBSE/AFF/CIRCULAR/2015/1393058 dated 21.06.2018 has 
already issued advisory to schools to not to coerce parents/ students for buying the books, 
stationery, uniforms or any other items from the schools tuck shop or from any other specified 
vendors. Further, schools have been directed to not to conduct any activity in the school premises 
which is wholly unconnected with the education. The schools have also been directed to display 
class-wise details of prescribed textbooks on its website before start of each academic session. 
  The Board vide circular no No. CBSE/Aff./Circular/2024/00976 dated 12.08.2024 has also 
categorically advised to the schools to follow NCERT/ SCERT textbooks for classes I to VIII. 
Schools may use supplementary material as per their requirement which must be aligned with the 
NCF-FS and NCF-SE. The schools have been directed to mandatorily follow the NCERT 
textbooks prescribed in CBSE curriculum for classes IX to XII. For subjects in which NCERT/ 
SCERT books are not available, CBSE books uploaded on the website must be followed. Schools 
can use supplementary material as per their requirement. 
  A new clause 2.4.7.1 has been added in the Affiliation Bye-Laws of the Board which 
stipulates that “Schools shall put a list of prescribed books for all the classes on their website with 
the written declaration duly signed by the Manager and the Principal to the effect that they have 
gone through the contents of the books prescribed by the school and own the responsibility. If a 
school is found prescribing a book having any objectionable content, the responsibility for such 
content shall lie with the school and action will be initiated against the School by the Board.” 
  In case, if any complaint pertaining to the violation committed by the school in this regard 
is received then the Board initiates appropriate action including holding inspection against such 
violating schools. In case, the violation(s) is established then the appropriate action as per chapter 
12 of the Affiliation Bye-Laws -2018 of the Board is initiated which may levied upto a maximum 
penalty of Withdrawal of Affiliation of the erring school. " 
Education is a subject in the Concurrent List of the Constitution. Schools, other than those 
owned/funded by the Central Government, are under the jurisdiction of the respective State 
Governments. Therefore, matters relating to fees charged by private schools and related issues are 
regulated in terms of Rules and Instructions of the respective State Government concerned. 
Various States have enacted distinct legislation, regulations, and laws to regulate fee structures in 
private educational institutions within their respective jurisdictions. 
However, under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 
2009, every child, of the age of six to fourteen years, has a right to free and compulsory 
elementary education in a neighbourhood school. Section 12(1) (c) of the RTE Act, 2009 
mandates reservation in private unaided schools for children belonging to weaker sections and 
disadvantaged groups to the extent of at least 25% seats at entry level and provision of free and 
compulsory elementary education to such children till its completion.

25. The Committee is of the view that to secure rights to these children, we must develop a 
robust protocol to identify and mainstream OoSc children. The Department should conduct a 
review of the protocols enforced by States across the country – like the well-regarded protocol in 
Karnataka and suggest a model set of rules for all States. Some features may include  
• The current definition of a drop-out is pegged at 45 days of unexcused absence. This 
extended period delays the detection and flagging of the prospective drop-out until two-
three months after the fact, a crucial time period in which the child may have migrated 
out, or engaged in work. The Karnataka protocol defines a ‘drop-out’ as a child with 
‘unexcused absence of seven days.’ This shortened time-span allows for a more proactive 
response rather than a reactive response 
• The Karnataka protocol places accountability on a specific designated state official – an 
‘attendance authority’ – who is tasked with ensuring that the Child Welfare Committee 
addresses the reason for the drop-out in a timely manner and mainstreams all local OoSc 
children within a specified time-frame 
• Currently, there is no instiutionalised or statutory mechanism for ensuring that child gets 
education if measures instituted by the Child Welfare Committee fail to bring back a child 
to school. In such cases, it may be appropriate for the state to take charge of the child 
and place them in a residential school 
(Para 3.4.47ibid)

27. The Committee recognizes that large parts of India are disaster-prone, with recurring 
natural disasters on an annual basis – including floods in Assam and parts of Bihar, landslides 
in eco-sensitive regions of the Western Ghats and Himalayas, and cyclones on the eastern coast 
of the country. However, it notes that there is no existing, comprehensive policy guidance on how 
school education should respond to a natural disaster. There is a need to do so given that most 
schools become relief camps in the event of a disaster, and schooling activities come to a stop, 
sometimes for months at a time. This leads to a learning loss, in addition to damage to school 
property. Accordingly the Committee recommends the formulation of a policy for school 
education in disaster-hit areas in coordination with Ministry of Home Affairs and the National 
Disaster Management Authority. Some features of this policy could include – 
 Provision for additional textbooks and uniforms in disaster-hit areas; 
 Extension of financial provisions for schools in disaster-hit areas, encompassing not just 
the structure but also the fixtures and furnishing; 
 Examination relief for students in disaster-hit communities, who cannot give exams on 
the same timeline as the rest of the state or country; 
 An assessment of the learning loss that occurs in such areas and formulation of a strategy 
to minimise the damage in the medium-term; and 
 Integration of disaster management into curriculum. 
(Para 3.4.50ibid)

28. The Committee reiterates the importance of Article 350(a) of the Indian Constitution, 
which mandates that the state shall endeavour to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the 
mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children belonging to linguistic minority 
groups. It also emphasises Article 29 of the Indian Constitution, which guarantees minority 
(linguistic, ethnic, and/or religious) communities the Fundamental Right to conserve culture, 
language and script, and administer educational institutions of their choice. The Committee 

28 
 
observes that the NEP acknowledges the importance of teaching students in the mother tongue, 
especially in the early years. However, by arguing that “[H]ome language is usually the same 
language as the mother tongue or that which is spoken by local communities,” the NEP doesn’t 
adequately grapple with the circumstance of linguistic minorities who speak a language different 
from that of their state and/or region. As a result, as the Department has acknowledged, 
Samagra Shiksha has no special focus or programs for students belonging to linguistic 
minorities. This has a cascading impact on state-level policies to support linguistic minorities. 
For instance, Maharashtra – which has ~4.6 lakh Gondi speakers as of 2011 – does not have a 
single Gondi-medium school. 
(i) Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Department should create a special 
program within Samagra Shiksha that supports states in the following – 
(ii) Coordinate with NCERT, NBT, and SCERT to ensure that TLM and all other resources 
are widely available (online for free and marketable) in all key languages – especially 
those spoken by Adivasi and tribal communities; 
(iii) Develop and financially support bridge courses to teach the state’s dominant language as 
a second language to children belonging to linguistic minorities; 
(iv) Develop pedagogy, teacher training, and TLM for instruction in multiple languages; and 
(v) Support recruitment of new teachers from the local linguistic communities that the school 
caters to. 
(Para 3.4.51 ibid) 
Action Taken 
National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, brought out after a nationwide deliberation with 
all stakeholders, teachers, parents, students and others, has recommended the promotion of all 
regional languages in school education. The NEP 2020 underscores the importance of 
recognising the linguistic diversity of the country which has a bearing and benefit in education 
and for multicultural understanding. Multilingualism as the policy and strategy has been 
emphasised in order to promote and strengthen the use of all Indian languages in school 
education from the early years of learning. The language section of the Policy has been titled, as 
Multilingualism and the Power of Language.  
The policy focuses on the mother tongue-based multilingualism as it states “it is well 
understood that young children learn and grasp nontrivial concepts more quickly in their home 
language/mother tongue”. 
Inclusion of languages of all learners in school curriculum is one major objective of the 
National Education Policy 2020 and National Curriculum Framework for Foundational Stage 
(NCF-FS) 2022 and National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCF-SE) 2023. 
National Education Policy 2020 states, ‘The three-language formula will continue to be 
implemented while keeping in mind the Constitutional provisions, aspirations of the people, 
regions, and the Union, and the need to promote multilingualism as well as promote national 
unity. However, there will be a greater flexibility in the three-language formula, and no language 
will be imposed on any State.  
The National Curriculum Framework for School Education, prepared in pursuance of 
NEP 2020, aims to enable all our students to learn at least three languages, fully leveraging our 
socio-cultural context and resources. 

29 
 
As per NCF-SE, the language in which literacy is first acquired in school (R1) will be the 
language that the student already knows, because that enables the full use of the linguistic and 
cultural knowledge (and resources) from one’s home and community. Further, our students will 
learn two more languages (R2 & R3). At least two of these three languages, R1, R2, and R3, 
must be native to India. The state or other relevant bodies would decide the choices of R1, R2, or 
R3 that would be given to students. 
The CBSE has issued guidelines to help schools implement the language-related 
recommendations of the National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCF-SE) 2023 
from the academic session 2025-26. According to the guidelines, in the early years of schooling 
called the Foundational and Preparatory stages, children should be taught in a language they 
understand well. It should ideally be their mother tongue or home language (called R1). If that is 
not possible, then a familiar regional or state language should be used. This first language (R1) 
should be the medium of instruction for all subjects until students have learned to read and write 
in another language (R2). 
Children with special needs must be given extra support, including extra time in exams, 
the option of using scribes, and exemptions from second or third language studies, as per the 
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. 
 
Primers in Indian Languages 
Primer is instructional material in book form – it is the first book for learners to learn and 
get familiar with the language as well as to notice and use language in contexts. The focus of 
primers is to introduce the letters of the alphabets, words and word chunks in real life contexts 
and also numbers and short sentences in the languages. Primers have been developed in tribal 
and indigenous languages of India as listed in the Census of India 2011. Central Institute of 
Indian Languages (CIIL), Mysuru and NCERT have jointly so far developed Primers supporting 
17 Scheduled, 23 Non-tribal, and 81 Tribal languages across 28 states/UTs, ensure linguistic 
inclusivity and accessibility, promoting lifelong learning and bridging educational gaps. The

schools through the avenue of this scheme; and

 Clear and strict guidelines are in place to ensure the academic and non-partisan nature of

31. Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE)-The Committee observes that 90% of an 
infant’s brain development occurs between 2-5 years. Universal ECCE, as envisioned in the NEP 
is therefore critical to securing lifelong thinking and reasoning capabilities for all of India’s 
children. However, the Committee observes that universal ECCE by 2030, as envisioned by NEP, 
remains a distant dream five years after the adoption of the NEP. The Committee regrets that the 
Kasturirangan Committee’s recommendation that ECCE be an integral part of RTE Act did not 
find space in the NEP. It therefore strongly recommends the expansion of the RTE to include 
ECCE for children aged 3 years to 6 years. The Committee is deeply concerned about the limited 
progress the Ministry has made in achieving universal ECCE. Physical convergence of Bal 
Vatikas and Primary Schools with Anganwadis has not occurred. More importantly, neither has 
operational convergence. The Committee observes that children enrolled in Bal Vatikas (pre-
schools in the Education Department) get mid-day meals through PM POSHAN while those in 
Anganwadis get it through the Saksham Anganwadi scheme. In Anganwadis, children are offered 
a welcome snack in addition to the meal. Children in Bal Vatikas get only a meal. Nutritional 
guidelines for both appear to be different, as are the cost norms SEL has prepared the Integrated 
Teacher Education Program for ECCE and NISHTHA ECCE. However, Anganwadi workers are 
being trained by NIPCCD under Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi scheme. The Committee is very keen on 
ensuring that regardless of which department runs the ECCE program, children need to be 
guaranteed the same food and the teachers need to be trained in a standardized fashion. The 
Committee also emphasizes that ECCE includes early childhood care and education – care is an 
integral part of what must be available to children, and Anganwadi workers are therefore part of 
the solution. The Department must work with the WCD Ministry to achieve universal ECCE. The 
Committee observes that Department of SEL and WCD have created a Joint Task Force to 
implement universal ECCE, but it appears to be ineffective. Given the demonstrated inadequacy 
of the two departments concerned, i.e., SEL and WCD, in making progress on universal ECCE, 

33 
 
the Committee recommends a national-level mission under the supervision of the PM to 
operationalize and accelerate convergence between the Bal Vatikas and Anganwadis. 
(Para 3.4.55ibid) 
Action Taken 
 The Department of School Education & Literacy (DoSE&L) have taken several steps for 
convergence between DoSE&L & Ministry of Women & Child Development (MoWCD): 
(i) Para 1.9 of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisions that Early Childhood Care 
& Education (ECCE) will be “carried out jointly by the Ministries of HRD, Women and 
Child Development (WCD), Health and Family Welfare (HFW), and Tribal Affairs”. To 
fulfil this vision, the DoSE&L have constituted a Joint Task Force (JTF) along with the 
MoWCD and other line Ministries. The JTF on ECCE works towards continuous guidance 
for the smooth integration of ECCE into school education that includes operationalizing and 
accelerating convergence between the Balvatikas and Anganwadis. JTF meetings are 
conducted at regular intervals. 
(ii) The JTF is in the process of finalizing the draft guidelines on co-location of Anganwadis. 
(iii) Meeting at the level of the Hon’ble Ministers of Education & WCD has been conducted 
along with the meetings between the Secretaries of the two Departments. 
(iv) Working together, a joint advisory by the Secretaries of DoSE&L & MoWCD has been 
issued on 02.04.2025, to all States/UTs on co-location of Anganwadis and improving the 
delivery of ECCE & FLN services across the country. 
 
Recommendation

33. The Committee takes note of the 2022 amendment to Section 20 of the RTE, which 
mandates schools to have 1 special education teacher for every 10 CwDs for classes 1 to 5, and 
1 special education teacher for every 15 CwDs for classes 6 to 8. While many states have already 
successfully sought grants for the same, the Committee strongly recommends the earmarking of 
specific funds through Samagra Shiksha for conducting a systematic census based identification 
exercise of CwD (Children with Disabilities), the hiring of special educators in all schools, and 
the training of special educators. Based on the identification exercise held by states, more funds 
may need to be dedicated to the hiring of special educators. 
(Para 3.4.57ibid) 
Action Taken 
Specific provisions as recommended by the Committee are already available under Samagra 
Shiksha for identification of CwD and engagement and training of special educators. More 
specifically; 
(i) Under Samagra Shiksha, all the States and Union Territories (UTs) are required to conduct 
Household Survey or updation of the household data annually for identification of out of 
school children including Children with Special Needs (CwSN). The survey is primarily 
conducted by the school teachers under the supervision of Head Teacher or Cluster/Block 
Resource Coordinator. Education Volunteers, Anganwadi Workers, Community Based 
Organizations, Members of School Management Committees (SMCs), Members of 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRI) etc.; are involved in this identification exercise. 
(ii) Annual camps for identification of CwSN are conducted at block level, followed by 
appropriate educational intervention based on the assessment. These camps are supported 
under Samagra Shiksha.  Total 19,766 block level identification and assessment camps were 
approved under Samagra Shiksha for the year 2025-26. 
(iii) To facilitate early identification, the PRASHAST Screening App containing the Pre-
Assessment Holistic Screening Checklist for Schools was launched on 6th September 2022. 
This is a scientific screening checklist to be used by regular teachers at all levels of 
schooling, to screen all school children at the earliest, so that the school wise disability 
screening data is shared with authorities, for further use in assessment and certification 
camps. The app collates the school level screening data of 21 disability conditions 
recognized in RPwD Act 2016. Till date (9th April 2025), more than 75.99 lakh students 
have been screened through PRASHAST. 
(iv) Financial support for engaging special educators (to meet PTR norms as prescribed by 
gazette notification) is provided to the States/UTs under Samagra Shiksha based on their 
proposal in AWP&B for the scheme of respective years.  However, the recruitment of 
teachers including special educators, their service conditions including monitoring of 
absence and deployment come under the purview of the respective State Governments and 
Union Territory administrations.  
(v) Regular capacity-building programs are conducted for special educators, along with training 
for general teachers on inclusive education to enhance their effectiveness for teaching in

inclusive classrooms. Under Samagra Shiksha, financial support is provided to the 
States/UTs every year for in-service training of special educators on cross-disability. In the 
year 2024-25, financial support amounting to ₹1034.45 lakh was provided to all 36 
States/UTs.

35. The Committee notes that the Department runs the Foundational Learning Study (FLS) 
and the National Assessment Survey (NAS) to evaluate student learning outcomes nationally. 
However, it recommends that their methodologies be standardized and rationalized – 
• NAS numeracy tests at Grade 3 include three-digit numbers and operations, which is 
beyond the scope of many children’s learning capacity 
• Literacy assessments in NAS focus only on reading comprehension, but need to 
incorporate the critical sub-skills of vocabulary and phonics essential for reading 
proficiency 
NAS should be redesigned to conduct one-on-one oral assessments as used in the FLS – this 
enables deeper evaluation of FLN skills and identification of gaps and learning difficulties. 
   
(Para 3.4.61ibid) 
Action Taken 
 The assessment framework of PARAKH RashtriyaSarvekshan 2024 (PRS 2024) has been 
aligned with the National Education Policy (NEP)2020, the National Curriculum Framework for 
Foundational Stage (NCF-FS) and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education 
(NCF-SE) and serves as a baseline for evaluating learning competencies acquired at different 
stages of schooling (foundational, preparatory and middle)under NEP. 
The test items administered for Grade 3 under PARAKH RashtriyaSarvekshan 2024, to 
evaluate learning competencies related to mathematics at the end of foundational stage, included 
only two-digit numbers- no test items involving three-digit numbers or operations were included.  
In order to scale assessment, PRS 2024 adopted the format of a multiple-choice question 
(MCQ) test conducted in a group setting. Through a MCQ based group test, it is not feasible to 
assess critical sub-skills such as decoding, phonics and vocabulary, which require one-on-one 

36 
 
interactive setting, in-depth. To this end, Foundational Learning Study (FLS) is separately 
conducted by NCERT so as to assess foundational literacy and numeracy through a detailed, task-
based, one-on-one assessment model. 
PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan and Foundational Learning Study serve distinct but 
complementary purposes.  
While PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan offers a broad, system-level snapshot of learning 
competencies across the country, Foundational Learning Study is designed specifically to deeply 
assess foundational literacy and numeracy skills through individual oral assessments. Given the 
scale and scope of PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan (which covered~6 lakh students in Grade 3 
vis-à-vis 84,000 under Foundational Learning Study 2022), converting it into one-on-one format 
online of Foundational Learning Study would entail considerable resources and logistics; hence, 
for the time being both assessments continue to operate in parallel to inform policy and practice 
effectively. 
 
Recommendation 
36. The Committee recommends that the Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas be expanded, 
particularly in ST-majority districts like Jhargram, including the Nayagram Block and Bandwan

(Para 3.4.65ibid) 
Action Taken 
 Under Samagra Shiksha, there is a provision of Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas 
(KGBVs). KGBVs are residential schools from Class VI to XII for girls belonging to disadvantaged 
groups such as SC, ST and OBC. 
The objective behind establishing KGBVs is to ensure access and quality education to girls 
from disadvantaged groups and to reduce gender gaps at all levels of school education. Target group 
for KGBVs is the girls in the age group of 11–18 years aspiring to study in Classes VI to XII SEDGs. 
There are 4 KGBVs functional in the Jhargram District, West Bengal with a total enrolment 
of 473 girl students. There are 8 blocks in Jhargram District and out of these 8 blocks, only 2 blocks 
(Nayagram and Gopiballavpur I) have 4 KGBVs..Bandwan Block is in the District of Purulia which 
has 1 functional KGBV.

37. The Committee notes that teachers are at the heart of the NEP – and none of the ideas 
discussed in the policy are possible without re-establishing “teachers, at all levels, as the most 
respected and essential members of our society” (NEP). The Committee believes that the first 
step towards restoring the status of teachers is to ensure that all teachers have the same service 
conditions, regarding pay, in-service teacher-training, transfers and other benefits. The dual 
system of regular teachers and contractual teachers creates a system of different pay for equal 
work, which goes against the spirit of the constitutional guarantee of equal pay for equal work. 
The hiring of contractual teachers also undermines the Constitutional right of SCs, STs, and 
OBCs to reservation in public employment. The Committee notes that the NEP 2020, unlike the 
draft version released in 2019, does not make any unequivocal statement on discontinuing the 
practice of hiring contract teachers. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department 
direct the utilisation of Samagra Shiksha funds by states towards the hiring of regular teachers 
alone, or the regularisation of contractual teachers. The Department must develop a clear 
roadmap for transitioning contractual teachers into permanent positions within the next five 

37 
 
years. States must also be encouraged to count years on contract as being part of a teacher’s 
service when considering promotions. 
(Para 3.4.66ibid) 
Action Taken 
Education being a subject in the Concurrent List of the Constitution, an overwhelming 
majority of the schools in the country comes under the administrative control of States/UTs. Their 
recruitment, service conditions come under the administrative purview of the respective State/UT 
concerned. 
All state/UTs are expected to have a permanent and professional cadre of subject-wise 
teachers. Ad hoc or temporary appointments of teachers need to be discouraged. Ad hoc or 
temporary appointments without following the regular recruitment process almost invariably 
result in poorly qualified teachers causing adverse impact on quality of education. To mitigate 
such concerns, a technology-based comprehensive teacher-requirement planning and forecasting 
exercise needs to be conducted by the States/UTs to assess expected subject-wise teacher 
vacancies and accordingly recruitment of qualified teachers. Recruitment methods and processes 
largely affect the selection of quality teachers. Apart from NCTE guidelines and Teacher 
Eligibility Tests (TETs), competitive selection examination with due care for consistency and 
sanctity is one of the major strategies to bring quality teachers. The recruitment can either be 
entrusted to State Public Service Commission (SPSC) or can be done by education department by 
establishing a central recruitment unit. 
The progress regarding filling up of teacher vacancies through a competitive selection 
examination conducted by States/UTs on a mission mode, with due care for consistency and 
sanctity and after a technology based comprehensive teacher requirement planning and forecasting 
exercise, is periodically reviewed through regular meetings with States/UTs as well as through 
advisories. 
The Department vide letter dated 24th March, 2025 has shared the model recruitment rules 
for academic and non-academic posts in schools with States/UTs requesting them to update their 
existing recruitment rules appropriately. 
 
Recommendation

Action Taken 

45 
 
PM SHRI Schools are set up by strengthening the existing schools from amongst schools 
managed by Central government/State/UT Government/local bodies. These schools are to 
showcase all the initiatives of National Education Policy 2020 and emerge as exemplar schools 
over a period of time, and also offer leadership to other schools in the neighbourhood. They 
provide leadership in their respective regions in providing high-quality education in an equitable, 
inclusive and joyful school environment that takes care of the diverse background, multilingual 
needs, and different academic abilities of children and makes them active participants in their 
own learning process as per the vision of NEP 2020. 
As per PM SHRI scheme guidelines,  
 “PM SHRI schools are envisioned to be exemplar in their regions, further helps to mentor 
schools in a given region with an aim to amplify the excellence of these schools and 
develop the quality standards of the PM SHRI Schools within these schools. This helps in 
handholding, collaboration and clustering, finally leading to a ripple effect for developing 
more potential exemplar schools every year.” 
 Also, these schools aim to act as a network of exemplar schools that will demonstrate 
excellence and act as belief, practices and knowledge centres for the entire learning 
ecosystem. PM SHRI schools may invite other schools in the same cluster or block to 
visit these exemplar schools to facilitate knowledge sharing and school improvement 
conversations.  
 Regular visits in the PM SHRI Schools by other schools in the district/block/cluster or 
nearby sub-locality to be encouraged to motivate them to adopt the interventions and 
become exemplar schools themselves. 
 
Thus, PM SHRI Scheme already provides, within its guidelines, for exemplar PM SHRI 
schools to offer leadership and mentorship to nearby government schools. The scheme actively 
supports the transformation of neighbourhood schools through structured collaboration, school 
visits, and cluster-based engagement. By positioning PM SHRI schools as exemplar schools to 
provide leadership and mentorship in the region, the scheme ensures that quality improvements 
extend to neighbourhood schools, enabling nearby schools to evolve through guided support.

            PM SHRI scheme showcases the initiative of National Education Policy (NEP) which 
allows States the flexibility to adopt their own education models while still benefiting from 
infrastructure and resource allocation. The following provisions of NEP 2020 reinforce this 
flexibility: 
i. As per Para 4.32 of NEP 2020, “States will prepare their own curricula (which may be 
based on the NCFSE prepared by NCERT to the extent possible) and prepare textbooks 
(which may be based on the NCERT textbook materials to the extent possible), 
incorporating State flavour and material as needed”. 
ii. Para 4.13 of NEP 2020 allows States and students choice in language learning under the 
three-language formula. It states, “The three-language formula will continue to be 
implemented while keeping in mind the Constitutional provisions, aspirations of the 
people, regions, and the Union, and the need to promote multilingualism as well as 
promote national unity. However, there will be a greater flexibility in the three-language 
formula, and no language will be imposed on any State. The three languages learned by 
children will be the choices of States, regions, and of course the students themselves, so 

48 
 
long as at least two of the three languages are native to India. In particular, students who 
wish to change one or more of the three languages they are studying may do so in Grade 6 
or 7, as long as they are able to demonstrate basic proficiency in three languages 
(including one language of India at the literature level) by the end of secondary school.”  
iii. Para 4.14 of NEP 2020 provides that, “All efforts will be made in preparing high-quality 
bilingual textbooks and teaching-learning materials for science and mathematics, so that 
students are enabled to think and speak about the two subjects both in their home 
language/mother tongue and in English.” 
iv. Para 4.35 of NEP 2020 mandates that, “The progress card of all students for school-based 
assessment, which is communicated by schools to parents, will be completely redesigned 
by States/UTs under guidance from the proposed National Assessment Centre, NCERT, 
and SCERTs.” 
Therefore, NEP 2020 provides considerable flexibility to States to adopt their own models 
while implementing various provisions of the policy. Funds are allocated under Samagra Shiksha 
to various States according to the available Budgetary allocation. For the year 2024-25, the 
Project Approval Board had approved the Annual Work plan & Budget Proposals of Rs. 855.90 
crore, Rs. 4305.66 crore and Rs. 3575.74 crore for the States of Kerala, Tamil Nadu & West 
Bengal respectively. However, the States of Kerala, Tamil Nadu & West Bengal have not 
expressed willingness to implement all provisions of NEP 2020. As a result, these States have not 
been able to avail the approved funds under Samagra Shiksha.

 Under PM SHRI scheme, central share of the funds approved for States/UTs by the

As per the Samagra Shiksha scheme guidelines, “Every School should constitute a School 
Management Committee (SMC/SMDC) which will include representatives of local authorities, 
academicians, subject experts, officials, representatives of disadvantaged groups, women and 
parents/guardians of students, in accordance with the RTE Act. The SMCs/SMDCs are expected

The role of the SMC/SMDC includes:

initiatives aimed at enhancing their ability to contribute to student enrolment, attendance, 
performance, governance, innovation, and community-led monitoring. 
iii. Annual Training: At the beginning of each academic year, training sessions for 
SMC/SMDC members are organized by the school staff to enhance their understanding of 
their roles and responsibilities. 
iv. School safety: Community mobilization funds are used to raise awareness among 
community members regarding safety protocols during school operations, especially in the 
context of emergencies, ensuring the security and well-being of students.

52. The Committee observes that despite India’s push for universal literacy, adult literacy

(iii) Customized Literacy Models: Tailored learning pathways should be developed for 
marginalized groups, including women-led literacy circles and tribal education modules

THE NATIONAL MISSION ON FOUNDATIONAL LITERACY AND NUMERACY 
(NIPUN BHARAT MISSION)  
Recommendation 
57. The Committee observes that foundational literacy and numeracy skills are critical for 
long-term educational success. However, fund underutilization and insufficient per- teacher 
allowances have limited the program’s reach and its impact. Strengthening implementation 
mechanisms can accelerate the improvement of literacy rates and numeracy competencies across 
the States. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the Department of School Education and 
Literacy as under:-   
(i) Annual Literacy & Numeracy Assessments: The Department should conduct 
standardized, state-level competency assessments, ensuring targeted interventions for 
underperforming schools; 
(Para 4.3.4ibid) 
Action Taken 
As per Para 4.41 of NEP a National Assessment Centre, PARAKH (Performance Assessment, 
Review, and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development), has been set up   as a standard-

58 
 
setting   body under DoSE&L that fulfils the basic objectives of setting norms, standards, and 
guidelines for student assessment and evaluation for all recognized school boards of India, 
guiding the State Achievement Survey (SAS) and undertaking the National Achievement Survey 
(NAS).  
The primary objective of this survey is to evaluate the learning competencies of students in 
Foundational Literacy, Foundational Numeracy, Language and Mathematics at the end of each of 
the educational stages i.e. Foundational, Preparatory, and Middle. The SEAS-23 has included 
blocks in the sample to cover of students to understand the learning gaps at the block level, a 
strategic shift from district. Approximately 8.4 million students and 6 lakh teachers, of 4 lakh 
schools of 6416 educational blocks were assessed in SEAS-23.  
The latest round of NAS, the PARAKH RashtriyaSarvekshan 2024 was conducted on 
December 4, 2024 by the National Assessment Centre, PARAKH. This survey marks a 
significant advancement in India’s assessment framework, aligning with the objectives of the 
National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which emphasizes competency-based learning and 
assessment reforms. The survey was designed to provide a detailed, granular understanding of 
student learning, at the end of Foundational, Preparatory and Middle stages, across different 
socio-economic backgrounds and regional contexts, ensuring that educational policies are data-
driven and targeted towards equitable learning improvements. With participation of 74000 
Schools, 2.70 lakh teachers and 21 lakh students from Government, Aided and Private Schools, 
the survey’s data collection and analysis are expected to yield significant insights into student 
learning competencies and the effectiveness of various interventions undertaken at the District, 
State and National levels. The findings will contribute to refining teacher training programs, 
curriculum reforms and state-specific strategies to bridge learning gaps. 
The Holistic Progress Card (HPC) has been introduced as a formative assessment tool to 
provide a multidimensional view of student progress. It goes beyond academics to include co-
curricular and socio-emotional development. Insights from these assessments guide evidence-
based interventions, ensuring uniform progress across all regions.

(Para 4.3.8ibid) 
Action Taken 
NEP 2020 gives a framework of 5+3+3+4 where the initial 5 pertains to 3 years of preschool 
education and Grade 1 and 2, translating to age group of 3-8 years. The NCF-FS also covers the same 
5 years in the education continuum of 15 years and accordingly text books for FS have been made for 
upto Grade 2. The ECCE also covers the age of 0-8 years where 0 to 3 years is home-based. NIPUN-
Bharat Mission is therefore now aligned to the above and covers age 3-8 years for 3 years of 
Balvatika Grade1 & Grade2. The earlier L.Os were focused on Grade 3 for ORF  with emphasis on 
reading on the parameter of words per minute. They were based on findings of Foundation stage 
survey done by NCERT and varied for all languages. 
There was no similar parameter for Grade 2. In this background, the Learning 
Outcomes(L.Os) or Lakshyas on various parameters for NIPUN Grades  have been redefined by 
NCERT in alignment with the National Education Policy(NEP), 2020, NCF-FS and NIPUN 
Guidelines. These are on the parameters of oral language, Reading, Writing and Numeracy.

66. The Committee further recommends the NCERT to ensure curriculum revision reflecting

Action Taken 
As a follow-up of NEP 2020, NCERT has brought our NCF for Foundational Stage and 
NCF for School Education. Both the curriculum documents provide adequate space to regional 
diversity, social inclusivity and technological advancements in curricular goals and competencies. 
These curriculum documents have been brought out with adequate public and expert consultation 
for curriculum development. Further to develop teaching-learning material including textbooks, 
National Syllabus and Teaching-Learning Material Committee(NSTC) and National Curriculum 
Framework Oversight Committee(NOC) including high level experts and scholars have been 
constituted followed by setting up of Curricular Area Groups and Textbook Development 
Committees. Regular engagements with experts, scholars and academia is continued for the 
development of textbooks. 
National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and National Curriculum Framework for School 
Education (NCF-SE) 2023 advocate the promotion India’s linguistic and cultural diversity in 
educational materials and processes. The NCERT’s Textbooks and other materials include 
materials / text/ stories, cultural artefacts and others are drawn from all Indian languages and 
culture. For example, Thirukkural has now been included in the textbooks of NCERT. 

65 
 
The content and illustrations included in these textbooks are gender neutral and gender 
sensitive that provide adequate space for promoting gender sensitivity among students. Every 
draft chapter of every newly developed NCERT textbook is discussed by the representatives of 
the cross-cutting Departments of the NCERT to ensure social inclusivity with no gender bias or 
any other form of discrimination anywhere in the textbooks. Some examples in Class 6 Social 
Science textbook, Exploring Society India and Beyond (Pg. 97) in the section ‘Let Us Explore’, 
all the students are asked to imagine a situation where they will be cooking a meal in an Harappan 
house, signifying that cooking is a life skill and not a gender role. One chapter also highlights a 
transgender person in a prominent role by exemplifying Dnyaneshwar Kabmle as an elected 
Sarpanch of Tarangfal village in Solapur district of Maharashtra (Pg.166). English textbook, 
Poorvi Grade 7, Unit 1, Learning Together, highlights the journey of a girl from the fields to the 
school and overcoming her fears to go to school. The chapter also gives a message that mentions, 
‘The happiness of a Nation lies in the dignity of its daughters’ and also shares many Government 
schemes for the education of the girl child such as ‘Beti Bachao Beti Padhao’, ‘Balika Samridhi 
Yojana’, ‘Samagra Shiksha Scheme–Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas’, etc. Other examples 
include; Unit 3, Dreams and Discoveries, that mentions about Dr. Janaki Ammal (Padma Shri), a 
brilliant woman scientist of India who made a significant contribution to the field of cytogenetics. 
Special Modules on Nari Shakti Vandan 
Besides, based on the principles of National Education Policy 2020 and guidelines of the 
National Curriculum Frameworks, the Department of Gender Studies in collaboration with faculty 
members of DEGSN, DEAA and DTE developed seven modules (in Hindi and in English) on 
Nari Shakti Vandan for students of various stages of school education. The following modules 
were developed: 1) Clever Annu 2) We are Second to None, 3) Empowering women: A Pathway 
towards progress and Development 4) Political Participation of Women for Equality and 
Development 5) Economic Empowerment of Women 6) Contribution of Women in Indian Arts 7) 
Contribution of Women in the Development of Society. These modules aimed to sensitize 
students and teachers on gender sensitivity as well as on varied aspects of women’s empowerment 
such as social, political, economic and contribution of women in Indian arts. These modules also 
highlight various initiatives to empower women in various aspects of life as well as for societal 
development. The modules are available on the NCERT website. 
Development of Training Module on Integrating Transgender Concerns in Schooling 
Process (A Module for Schools) 
Given that schools are one of the major change makers in the Indian education system with 
close and regular contact with the students, it becomes important to equip all the stakeholders to 
meaningfully engage with the emerging gender concerns. The module on Integrating Transgender 
Concerns in Schooling Process has been developed keeping in mind the concerns of inclusion of 
transgender in school education system with a whole school environment and sensitizing and 
equipping teachers, principals, school support staff, teacher educators, as well as other 
stakeholders to integrate students with diverse gender identities.  
One-Day Sensitisation Programme on Integrating Transgender Persons’ Concerns in 
Schooling Processes

stakeholders/master trainers to transform schools into inclusive spaces that uphold human rights,
