RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE -AT A GLANCE  
 
1. The Committee notes with appreciation that there is gradual increase in Centre and 
States expenditure in education which stood at 4.12% of GDP in 2021-22. However, there is 
a long way to go before it achieves the target of 6% of GDP. Given that the nominal GDP of 
the country at current prices is around 360 lakh crores which is likely to further increase in 
future, public investment and expenditure in education needs to be at least doubled from the 
current budget allocation of Rs 121118 crore in BE 2024-25 to achieve the target. The 
Committee therefore recommends the Department to argue its case assiduously before the 
Ministry of Finance for enhanced allocation for the Ministry. The Committee notes the reply 
of the Department that our spending in education as a percentage of DGP is higher than 
Russia and China. So far as Russia is concerned, as its population may be about 1/10 of 
India, its per capita investment or expenditure in education may still be much higher than 
us. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Department must draw up a time-bound, 
outcome-linked roadmap to progressively raise education expenditure to 6% of GDP, with 
clearly defined annual milestones. 
(Para 2.9& 2.10 ibid) 
2. The Committee is of the view that the figure of 11.7 lakh out of school children is 
considerably high. Such children have a constitutional as well as statutory right to have 
access to education and the state is obliged to provide the same. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends the Department to consider developing a national preventive protocol under 
RTE Rules, designating cluster-level Education Coordinators as attendance authorities to 
act within a predefined days of absence and involve Child Welfare Committees for chronic 
cases. Further, the Department should also consider making appropriate changes in 
centralized UDISE+ to integrate real-time OoSC tracking report, mandating monthly state 
reports and third-party audits. The Committee also recommends that the matter should be 
pursued with the states so that appropriate measures are taken in an expeditious manner for 
inclusion of such children in formal education system and inform the Committee 
accordingly. 
(Para 3.4.4 ibid) 
3. The Committee notes that the Department has acknowledged the issues in principle. 
However, the absence of enforceable timelines, accountability mechanisms, and funding-
linked incentives has resulted in stagnation in teacher recruitment. The Committee feels 
that keeping such large numbers of posts vacant for years together denies the students 
quality education and therefore is an infraction of the spirit of RTE Act. Given the 
magnitude of vacancies and their direct impact on learning outcomes, the Committee 
stresses that urgent action is needed in the larger national interest and for safeguarding the 
future of millions of school-going children. The Committee accordingly recommends that 
the Department should actively engage with the State Governments to sort out difficulties, 
if any, in filing up the vacancies as soon as possible.   
(Para 3.4.30, 3.4.31 & 3.4.32 ibid) 
 
4. The Committee notes that the funds due to Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Kerala 
have been duly approved by the Project Approval Board (PAB) of the Samagra Shiksha 
Abhiyan. The Committee appreciates that the Ministry is regularly engaging with the State 
Governments of Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Kerala to resolve the matter. The 
Committee recommends that the funds that have been approved may be released. 

112 
 
 
(Para 3.4.34 , 3.4.35 (i), (ii), (iv), (v) & (vi) ibid) 
 
5. The Committee is not convinced with the reply of the Department and recommends 
that the Department should analyse the recommendations of the Committee given in its 
Reports and accordingly formulate an action plan with focusing on the points given as 
under:- 
(i) The Department should make it mandatory for the Central/State Boards to audit all 
affiliated private schools annually for RTE compliance, including seat reservations, 
admissions, and entitlements. Publish a national dashboard of compliant/errant 
schools; 
(ii) The Department should commission a study by NCERT or NUEPA on RTE 
implementation in private schools (focusing on Section 12(1)(c)), covering 
admissions, entitlements, and dropout rates. This study should be completed at the 
earliest with policy guidelines based on findings; 
(iii) The Department should enhance Samagra Shiksha norms for real-time grievance 
redressal portals, mandatory school audits for entitlements, and compliance 
certification should be made essential  reimbursements; and 
(iv) Steps should be taken for annual training for private schools on RTE via Central 
Boards, coupled with public campaigns to encourage invitation of applications. 
(Para 3.4.41ibid) 
6. The Committee notes that Ministry of Education has issued guidelines to all States 
and UTs that emphasize teachers should not be deployed for non-educational duties other 
than those which are in accordance with the RTE Act, 2009. However, in actual practice, 
these guidelines are not followed. The Committee therefore recommends that proper 
guidelines should be framed and monitored through digital dashboard by integrating into 
the existing UDISE+ (Unified District Information System for Education) portal. States 
should also report the average time teachers spend on non-academic tasks. Further, a 
dedicated Grievance Redressal portal for Teachers should be developed where teachers can 
anonymously report being assigned duties that violate Section 27 of the RTE Act.  
(Para 3.4.46ibid) 
 
7. The Committee feels that while the data confirms the enrolment decline, the absence 
of analysis, investigation, and remedial action is a matter of serious concern. Given the 
constitutional commitment to social justice and inclusive education, the Committee is of the 
view that any decline disproportionately affecting disadvantaged communities should be 
addressed immediately. 
(Para 3.4.48ibid) 
8. The Committee is of the view that mere electricity connections on paper are 
meaningless in the absence of reliable and functional power supply. Given the centrality of 
electricity to modern schooling and NEP implementation, the Committee stresses that 
functional electrification must be treated as a core educational entitlement, supported by 
dedicated funding, rigorous monitoring, and clear accountability mechanisms. 
(Para 3.4.58ibid) 

113 
 
9. The Committee notes with great concern that the average rate of utilization of LEP 
funds by the states during FY 2023-24 was 18.66% and during FY2024-25 was 54.31% 
which means that most of the states are not able to even fully utilize even Rs,500/- per child 
per year allotted under the program. This pathetic rate of utilization of earmarked amount 
must have been seriously jeopardising the learning enhancement of such students who have 
somehow lacked behind acquiring skills and competences commensurate to their age or 
class and now has to do a remedial catch-up. The Committee therefore recommends the 
Department to find the reasons for such poor fund utilization by the states and help them in 
achieving full utilization of their allotted amount. 
(Para 3.4.59ibid) 
10. The Committee observes that merely seeking information from States/UTs is not 
going to address the structural fragmentation of student data systems. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that to realise the NEP 2020 vision of seamless, lifelong academic 
tracking and to strengthen dropout prevention and equity, the Department must move 
decisively from information-gathering to standard-setting, integration, and enforcement. A 
unified, interoperable student academic ID ecosystem anchored in APAAR is essential for a 
modern, inclusive education system. The Committee accordingly reiterates its earlier 
recommendation that Department should ensure the linking of these state IDs to the APAAR 
ID to ensure single unified data sets and interoperability. 
(Para 3.4.62ibid) 
 
11. The Committee expresses is concern that there still exists 22,298 unrecognised 
schools for more than three years in violation of the provisions of the RTE Act. This in the 
opinion of the Committee is a very serious matter as an unsuspecting student may end 
finding that the school from which he got education is not recognised by the government. 
This may cause crisis particularly for students appearing for Board Examination. The 
Committee therefore is the view that the Department should pursue the matter with the 
State Governments so that running of unrecognised schools is fully stopped immediately.  
(Para 3.4.63 ibid) 
 
12. The Committee is of the opinion that linking DIKSHA with UDISE+, APAAR, and 
Aadhaar is not merely a technical exercise but a critical enabler of outcome-oriented digital 
education policy. The current response of the Department though indicates intent but lacks 
specificity and urgency. The Committee therefore urges the Department to finish the task of 
linking the DIKSHA portal with UDISE+, Aadhaar, and APAAR ID at the earliest in order to 
fully realise the potential of DIKSHA as a national digital public good for education. 
(Para 3.4.64ibid) 
 
13. The Committee notes with concern that there still exists 1,10,971 single teacher 
schools in the country. The Committee understands that such schools often exist in remote 
and rural areas. The Committee further notes that the Department has taken several 
training, pedagogical and technical interventions to enable the teachers to handle multi 
grade teaching scenario. The  Committee however observes that one teacher managing 
multiple grades simultaneously not only makes the single teacher overloaded with academic 
and administrative work but also result in closure of school operations in case the teacher 
falls ill or remains absent for any other reason. While acknowledging the significance of 
such schools in catering to the educational needs of students in remote and far-flung areas 

114 
 
of the country, the Committee recommends that such schools should be converted into at 
least two teacher in a time bound manner. 
(Para 3.4.67ibid) 
 
14. The Committee feels that sudden stoppage of nutritional meal to students after class 
VIII, when most of them reach adolescence is like suddenly turning the tap off before the 
bucket is filled completely. Given that adolescence is a critical growth phase which requires 
increased nutritional intakes, proper nutrition during these years will go a long way in 
preventing a large number of long term health issues, reduce drop outs particularly 
amongst girls as the poor families are incentivised to keep their children in schools. The 
Committee therefore feels that there is a sustained need to integrate education with 
nutrition beyond class VIII. This is all the more needed as students have to prepare for 10th 
and 12th Board examinations which demands higher focus and cognitive performance.  The 
Committee therefore recommends the Department should increase the scope and coverage 
of the scheme to all the students up to class X then   take it to class XII in the next five 
years. 
(Para 3.5.10 (i) ibid) 
 
15. The Committee notes that the Department in its ATN has submitted that presently 
there is no plan to include breakfast under PM Poshan or extend the Scheme to students 
beyond class VIII. The Committee in this connection observes that breakfast being the first 
meal of the day is very crucial for students as it provides the essential energy for focus, 
improves memory and concentration and boosts academic performance. The Committee 
therefore recommends the department to introduce at least light breakfast in particular in 
the morning shift schools. The Committee further recommends that the Central and the 
State governments should gradually increase their share so that scope is created for proving 
an additional light meal along with the regular meal to all the students.  
(Para 3.5.10 (ii) ibid) 
 
16. The Committee observes that the honorarium of Rs. 1000/- per month of the CCHs 
has remained stagnant for almost two decades. The inflation and cost of living during this 
period has increased many folds. The Committee underscores that there is high work load 
on these CHHs as they are involved in procuring, cleaning and cooking and serving hot

the present honorarium is by and large far below the statutory minimum wages, the

(Para 3.5.10 (vii) ibid) 
 
17. The Committee takes note of the Department’s response regarding development of 
SQAF and ongoing evaluation by NITI Aayog. However, the Committee reiterates that

select schools. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should make a 
clear policy decision on extending PM-SHRI benefits to average government schools by 
suitably relaxing norms and reconsidering inclusion of KVs and JNVs. The Committee also 
expects the evaluation report to specifically highlight tangible improvements attributable to 
PM-SHRI status and their scalability across the wider public school system. 

115 
 
(Para 3.6.8ibid) 
18. The Committee is deeply concerned at the fact that the six targeted states are unable 
to fully spend their approved funds consistently over the years since the Scheme started in

(Para 3.7.6 ibid)

CHAPTER I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2025-26) OF THE 
MINISTRY OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS 
Recommendation 
1. The Committee was informed that the Department secures 0.02% of the Union 
Government’s budget. The Committee noted that this was lower than expected given that the 
country has a large youth population. Further, a large part of the increase in expenditure for the 
Department is due to one-time expenses, such as the Rs 64.26 crore incurred for the up 
gradation of the MY Bharat Portal. The Committee noted that the underutilization of funds in 
previous years weakens the Department’s case for a higher budget and recommends that the 
Department ensure full utilization of funds in the future.  
(Para 2.1.17 of the 366th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted.  
Due to roll out/implementation of TSA, release of NSS Grants to State NSS functionaries 
was delayed during FY 2024-25. However, in the current financial year (FY 2025-26), 
exemption to implement TSA has been accorded till 30 September 2025. As a result, 1st 
instalment of the NSS grant (25%) has already been released to most of the states and demand 
for 2nd instalment along with the UCs has been sought from the States by the Ministry so as to 
release further instalments of the Grant to the states.  The department aims to fully utilise the 
allotted fund this year. 
 Further, concerned Autonomous Bodies (ABS), attached offices & Program Divisions 
have been advised to ensure full timely utilization of funds in the future. 
NON-UTILIZATION OF BUDGET  
Recommendation 
2. The Committee queried as to why the RE for the FY 2024-25 was not utilized and as to 
why the BE for the FY 2025-26 was reduced when the resources were direly needed. The 
Committee notes that there is an increase in the budget outlay for the current financial year and 
recommends that the Department take all steps to ensure that the same is not repeated. 
 (Para 2.2.9 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. Further, concerned Autonomous Bodies 
(ABS), attached offices & Program Divisions have been advised to ensure full utilization of 
funds in the future. 
STREAMLINING OF NYKS PROGRAMMES THROUGH FLAGSHIP FOCUS AREAS 
Recommendation 
3. The Committee was informed that the Nehru Yuva Kendras ran at least 42 core 
programmes and 11 special programmes in the last few years. The Committee is concerned that 

 
3 
 
the proliferation of programmes and activities dilutes the brand of the NYKS. The Committee 
was informed that each year, the NYKS core programmes are set by the Annual Action Plan 
approved by the Board of Governors. The Committee recommends that the NYKS adopt a few 
flagship programs that are conducted every year without fail, so as to provide a focus to the 
organization and build its brand positioning among youth. Additional special programmes may 
be instituted as per the decision of the Board of Governors. 
(Para 2.2.10 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. 
Annual Action Plan of MY Bharat, which is an umbrella autonomous body, has been 
divided in five flagship focus areas and all programmes are designed around these focus areas – 
These focus areas are –  
 One Nation One Youth for Viksit Bharat 
 Youth Leadership for Viksit Bharat 
 Making India a sporting and Fit Nation for Viksit Bharat 
 Building Communities for Viksit Bharat 
 Vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 
TRACKING OF ALUMNI OF NYKS, NSS AND NYVS 
Recommendation 
4. The Committee was informed that the NYKS programs are designed to instill a sense of 
civic responsibility and build personality traits that help participants in their academic and 
professional journeys. However, the Committee was informed that there is currently no 
mechanism to track the professional trajectories of NYKS participants beyond their association 
with the NYKS. The Committee believes that tracking the alumni of the programs can help inform 
the Department about the long-term utility of the program, as well as create an alumni network 
that can benefit the existing volunteers. The same provision can be extended to NSS volunteers 
and NYVs as well. The Committee notes that the MY Bharat Platform has provided a dedicated 
profile page for each youth to describe their professional interest. For Experiential Learning 
Program conducted on the portal, a certificate of participation is also reflected on the youth 
profile page as an incentive to youth to update their profiles from time to time. This facility can 
be used to track the NYK volunteers, NSS volunteers, and NYVs after their association with the 
Department and its activities ends. 
(Para 2.2.11 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted.  
All NSS Volunteers across the country shall be registered on MY Bharat Portal and their 
profile may also be created to get the benefits of Experiential Learning Programme (ELPs) by 
the various Govt. Departments and agencies from time to time. On boarding of educational 
institutions on My Bharat is also being undertaken across the country as knowledge institutions 
(KIs). For tracking the alumni of NSS a study is being currently undertaken on similar lines as 
the NCC Alumni Association. NSS Alumni Association shall also be registered under the 
Society Regulations Act 1860. The future NSS Alumni Association would serve as a centralized, 

 
4 
 
national-level digital platform for alumni across India to register, network, engage and contribute 
to the NSS community. 
It is further proposed to create a special category on MY Bharat portal for registration of 
NSS, NYV and MY Bharat alumni. This shall enable tracking of the activities performed and 
possibilities for these alumni to act as future mentor. 
 
PROMOTION OF CONSTITUTIONAL VALUES IN YOUTH PROGRAMMES 
Recommendation 
5. The Committee noted with satisfaction that more than 2,000 Padyatras were organised 
across the country to commemorate the Constitution Day 2024 celebrating 75 years of Indian 
constitution, in which more than 1.5 lakh youth and others participated where oath of the 
Preamble to the Constitution was integral part of the Padyatra. The theme of these padyatras 
was Humaara Samvidhaan, Humaara Swabhimaan. On the same lines, the Committee 
recommends that all youth programs must begin with oath taking of the Preamble to the 
Constitution, and the recitation of the National Pledge. Similarly, all NYKS building and other 
structures operated by the Department must feature a copy of the Preamble to the Indian 
Constitution to build a culture of Constitutional morality among our youth. 
(Para 2.2.12 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion has been noted. Further in so far as NSS is concerned, it is informed that as 
per the commemoration of the Constitution Day on 26th November has been observed in all NSS 
Institutions in a grand manner by adopting the pledge taking and reading of the preamble of the 
Indian Constitution. Further, the communication has already been sent to all NSS Regional 
Directorates, State NSS Officers and the education institutes to follow the program with reading 
of the preamble of the constitution. The display of the Preamble of the Constitution has been 
installed at all NSS Offices. 
Communication sent to all MY Bharat Kendras, to begin such program with reading of the 
Preamble of the Constitution. The display of the Preamble of the Constitution shall also be done 
in all MY Bharat Kendras. 
ENHANCED ENGAGEMENT WITH DISTRICT COLLECTORS, STATE 
ADMINISTRATION AND ELECTED REPRESENTATIVES 
Recommendation 
6. The Committee recommends that the Department should work more closely with the 
District Collectors, the State administration, and elected representatives to involve them in 
programmes being conducted at the district level so that they can leverage their own networks to 
enhance youth participation in the schemes. 
(Para 2.2.13 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. As far as MY Bharat is concerned, it is 
informed that the district MY Bharat coordinates with district collectors, State Govt. departments 
on regular basis. District MY Bharat extends invitation to elected representatives in its 
programmes.  

 
5 
 
Further, NSS is a flagship programme under Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports which 
is being implemented in all the States through 15 Regional Directorates of NSS and State NSS 
Officers as field offices to implement the scheme in coordination with State Governments 
departments. The NSS Functionaries at Institution and State level are always coordinating with 
the district administration and urban local bodies for all kinds of community welfare and 
awareness programmes in the campus and community., e.g,: tree plantation drives, Shramdaan, 
Swachhata Hi Seva, Ek Ped Maa ke Naam campaign, Maati ko Naman Veero ka Vandan 
campaign, Health and Hygiene camps, women and child empowerment campaigns, environment 
awareness campaigns etc., are inaugurated by the elected public representatives (MPs, MLAs 
and Councillors of local bodies). 
CAPACITY BUILDING SUPPORT TO NYKS, NSS AND YOUTH CLUBS IN MANIPUR 
Recommendation 
7. The Committee notes the work done by NYKS, NSS, and local Youth Clubs in promoting 
peace and social harmony in Manipur, and in bringing Internally Displaced Persons into 62 
relief camps. The Committee encourages the Department to continue supporting these groups in 
these endeavours and to provide them with capacity building support to promote social harmony 
at the grassroots level. 
(Para 2.2.14 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted.  
Further, despite social unrest and prevailing situation in Manipur, the NSS Units have 
been actively carrying out activities with primary focus on community services. The committee 
suggestions will be complied with and NSS volunteers and functionaries shall be encouraged to 
be involved in capacity building support to promote social harmony and national integration at 
grassroots level. 
From Manipur, 18,706 youth volunteers and 45 youth clubs have registered on the MY 
Bharat portal. MY Bharat is providing a wide range of volunteering and experiential learning 
opportunities for young people. Some of the notable programs include celebrating important 
national days and weeks, the International Day of Yoga, Swachhta (cleanliness) programs, 
promoting sports through district and block-level sports programs, and experiential learning 
programs in collaboration with the Department of Post and All India Radio. 
IMPLEMENTATION OF NYV SCHEME AND COVERAGE ACROSS STATES/UTS 
Recommendation 
8. The Committee notes with concern that there is a steady decrease in the RE of the 
National Service Scheme as compared to its BE for the last four financial years – the RE in 
2021-22 was 89.48% of the BE; in 2022-23 it was 87.91%, in 2023-24 it was 72.07% and in 
2024-25 it was 72.05%. The Committee recommends that the Department look into the reasons 
for the same and ensure that the enhanced budget for FY25-26 is utilized fully. 
(Para 2.3.4 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. 

 
6 
 
It is submitted that due to roll out/implementation of TSA system, release of NSS Grants 
to State NSS functionaries was delayed during FY 2024-25. However, in the current financial 
year (FY 2025-26), exemption for CNA has been accorded till 30th September 2025. As a result, 
1st instalment of the NSS grant (25%) has already been released to most of the states and demand 
for 2nd instalment along with the UCs has been sought from the States by the Ministry so as to 
release the further instalments of the Grant to the states.  The department aims to fully utilise the 
allotted funds this year i.e., 2025-26. 
DEPLOYMENT OF NATIONAL YOUTH VOLUNTEERS UNDER MY BHARAT 
Recommendation 
9. The Committee notes that the National Youth Volunteers (NYVs) are the key 
implementers of this scheme since they work as a bridge between the youth and the field officers 
of the NYKS and MY Bharat. However, in the FY 2024-25, the Department was not able to reach 
the target number of NYVs and the scheme was implemented only in eight States and UTs. This 
must be avoided in the future. 
(Para 2.3.5 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. Efforts are being made to deploy the MY 
Bharat Youth Volunteers at all block levels.  
Recommendation of the Committee is kindly noted.  
REVISION OF HONORARIUM OF NATIONAL YOUTH VOLUNTEERS UNDER 
RYSK SCHEME 
Recommendation 
10. The Committee notes that during the EFC meeting for the continuation of RYSK scheme 
for the period from 2021-22 to 2025-26, all the seven schemes of RYSK including NYC were 
deliberated upon. The proposal of the Ministry for enhancing the honorarium of NYVs from Rs. 
5000/- to Rs. 15000/- was also discussed but not agreed to by the EFC. 
However, the Committee recommends that the Department continue to advocate for an 
increased honorarium of Rs. 15,000 per month for NYVs. 
(Para 2.3.6 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
The 3rd party assessment study has been initiated by the Department of Youth Affairs to 
review the RYSK Scheme and on the basis of the report that is to be received by the agency; the 
matter will be taken up in the next EFC with Ministry of Finance to enhance the honorarium. 
Department will also indicate the view of Committee in their EFC meetings.  
ADOLESCENT DEVELOPMENT AND WOMEN YOUTH LEADERSHIP UNDER 
NPYAD 
Recommendation 
11. The Committee recommends that the Department consider adolescents as a distinct sub-
group among the youth and address their distinct needs through this scheme. The Department 

 
7 
 
must also focus on developing leadership skills among women youth to challenge the 
misconception that the youth refers only to men. 
(Para 2.4.5 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. Further, as per the National Programme for 
Youth and Adolescent Development (NPYAD) Scheme Guidelines, ‘youth’ would cover persons 
belonging to the age group of 15-29 years and ‘adolescent’ would cover persons in the age group 
of 10-19 years.  Some of the activities for which grants-in-aid may be made under NPYAD 
Scheme towards development and empowerment of adolescents are Life Skills Education, 
Counselling, Career Guidance and Residential Camps.  
As regards development of leadership skills among women youth, women participants 
are given equal preference in all youth leadership programmes under MY Bharat and NSS. 
PROVISION OF E-LIBRARY FOR YOUTH IN NATIONAL YOUTH POLICY 
Recommendation 
12. The Committee recommends that the National Youth Policy must reflect the need for an 
e-library for youth, which brings together all digital resources, including key texts written by our 
freedom fighters and other national icons, for India’s youth. 
(Para 2.4.6 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
The recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing Committee has been noted and shall 
be kept in view at the time of formulating revised ‘National Youth Policy’. 
 
IMPROVING UTILISATION OF YOUTH HOSTELS BY STATES/UTS 
Recommendation 
13. The Department may make endeavour to impress upon the State/UT Govt. to formulate a 
plan for better utilization of these youth hostels. 
(Para 2.6.3a of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. 
RENOVATION AND MAINTENANCE OF YOUTH HOSTELS 
Recommendation 
14. The Committee notes that the physical maintenance of 84 Youth Hostels will not cost 
much, thus, both the Central and State Government, should make allocations for their annual 
maintenance. The revenue expenditure under the Youth Hostel sub-scheme have two components 
i.e. ‘Honorarium to Managers & Wardens’ and ‘Repair/ Renovation of Youth Hostels’. As per 
the Youth Hostel Manual, the responsibility of the repair, maintenance, and improvement in the 
building of the Youth Hostels is with the State/UT Governments. For alternations or major 
repairs to the building, if the State Government is unable to make available necessary funds, the 
Directorate of Youth Services & Sports of the State may refer it to Central Department for a 
grant. The Committee notes that the Department informed the Committee that “some of the youth 

 
8 
 
hostels are not in habitable conditions,” an observation which was corroborated by MPs. 
Accordingly, the Committee strongly recommends that funds should be provided by the 
Department for the renovation of youth hostels. 
(Para 2.6.4 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. Further, the Youth Hostel Scheme contains 
a provision to extend a need-based, one-time grant / financial assistance up to ₹20 lakh for 
renovation and upgradation of Youth Hostels, subject to receipt of viable proposals. For 
provision of grant additional to this Department of Youth Affairs will send a case DoE, Ministry 
of Finance indicating the recommendation of Hon’ble Committee.  
The Department is exploring options to manage Youth Hostels on a PPP mode, in order 
to expand coverage and provide affordable hostels to larger number of youth.  
EXPANSION OF YOUTH HOSTELS IN METROPOLITAN CITIES, STATE 
CAPITALS AND EDUCATIONAL CENTRES 
Recommendation 
15. The Committee notes that there are no youth hostels in NCT Delhi– although the 
Committee had specifically recommended it in all capitals. Similarly, the Committee notes that 
previous recommendations made by the Committee for hostels specifically for girl youth have not 
been accepted by the Department. It re-emphasizes the need for the same given the cultural 
sensitivities involved and the concerns around safety of female youth in these hostels. The 
Committee notes that there is acute shortage of youth hostels in the country, particularly in 
educational centres, which hurts the educational prospects of youth from low-income groups, 
girls, SCs, STs, OBCs, and EWS. The Committee, therefore, recommends that additional budget 
be made available for the construction of youth hotels in the four metropolitan cities, capital 
cities of each State, and centres of education for boys and girls separately to ensure the cheapest 
boarding facilities for the youth of the country. The Committee recommends that the Department 
seek additional funds from the Ministry of Finance for the same at RE 2025-26 stage. 
(Para 2.6.6 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Youth Hostel as per the manual is available for all youth, however suggestion of the Committee 
has been noted and shall be kept in view while taking a decision for construction of new Youth 
Hostels. While projecting for more funds to Ministry of Finance, Department will make them 
aware regarding recommendations of Hon’ble Committee.  
RE-DESIGNING YOUTH HOSTELS FOR YOUTH ENGAGEMENT AND 
ENTREPRENEURSHIP 
Recommendation 
16. The Committee was informed that in the recently concluded Viksit Bharat Young Leaders 
Dialogue in January, 2025, one of the key recommendations made by youth was the need to have 
more co-working spaces for young entrepreneurs in urban spaces. In order to meet the 
requirement of youth and for optimum utilization of the existing infrastructure, it may be planned 
to re-design Youth Hostels for constructive youth engagement and empowerment. 
(Para 2.7.3 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  

 
9 
 
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted for compliance. 
ENSURING OPTIMAL FUND UTILIZATION AND RURAL COMPONENT UNDER 
NYLP 
Recommendation 
17. The Committee notes that this dynamic platform was envisaged to empower young 
Indians to contribute their ideas and perspectives towards fulfilling the vision of Viksit Bharat. 
However, the funds utilization position shows that, under the Scheme, the expenditure as on 
31/01/25 is Rs. 4.01Crores only whereas the Revised Estimates for the FY 24-25 is Rs. 
6.00Crores. With regard to NYLP, the Committee noted that the rural component of the youth 
should not be lost sight of and every effort should be made to reach out to rural youth. 
(Para 2.7.5 of the 366th Report of the Committee)  
Action Taken 
Suggestion of the Committee has been noted for compliance. 
PROMOTING LEADERSHIP QUALITIES IN WOMEN YOUTH THROUGH NYLP, 
NSS AND NYKS 
Recommendation 
18. The Committee noted that there is no targeted and specific programme for inspiring 
leadership qualities in women youth. The example of women leaders of the past should be used 
to inspire the younger generations through the NYLP, as well as through the activities of the NSS 
and NYKS.

TALENT IDENTIFICATION, TRAINING, AND NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT IN 
SPORTS 
Recommendation 
26. The Committee recommends that the Department should integrate their strategy for 
talent hunt in all the games and sports with the National Sports Policy and that it should be 
synergized with the games at the school, district, state and national level. It should be continuous 
and ongoing process on yearly basis at all levels, so that sports talent is adequately identified

13 
 
requirement of athletes. However, it recommended that the Department give additional focus to

Extension Centers of STCs, and National Sports Talent Contest centers as well. The Committee 
recommended that places like Haryana, Manipur, Punjab, etc. which are famous for particular 
sports, need to be invested in to further develop the sports ecosystem in these states. 
(Para 5.3.11 of the 366th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
Under SAI Training Centres (STCs), the Department has a well-defined selection criteria 
for induction of athletes into the STCs. Athletes are considered for selection based on desirable 
performance in school, university, zonal, district, and national-level competitions, subject to 
being medically and physically fit and demonstrating potential through a battery of tests. This 
ensures that talent is identified at the grassroots and provided with structured training and 
support. Also, there are qualified Nutritionists at the Regional Centre level who prepare diet 
charts for athletes at STCs. The dietary requirements of athletes are regularly monitored by the 
respective Regional Centres to ensure nutritional adequacy and alignment with training loads. 
Further, the selection of athletes into NCOEs is undertaken by Talent Identification and 
Development Committees (TIDCs) specific to each sporting discipline. Athletes are selected 
through annual assessments based on their performance in national and international 
competitions. These shortlisted athletes are invited to assessment camps, where induction is 
conducted based on a comprehensive evaluation including Performance indicators, 
Anthropometric measurements, Physiological and psychological assessments. 
This robust process ensures that only athletes with the highest potential are inducted into 
the NCOEs. 
Also, the National Sports Talent Contest (NSTC) Scheme includes: 
 Medal winners at State/National level competitions are admitted, subject to medical 
fitness. 
 Medal winners at the District level or participants in State level competitions are also 
eligible, subject to being medically and physically fit and demonstrating potential through 
battery of tests. 
 
Through various components of Khelo India, talent is identified and nurtured. Khelo India 
Talent development component identifies meritorious athletes through various sets of 
competition including Khelo India Games and nurtures them. Apart from this, talent is nurtured 
at district level through over 1048 Khelo India Centres across the country. 
 
Significant steps have already been taken under Khelo India Scheme to address the 
Committee's recommendations regarding talent identification, financial assistance, and the 
development of sports ecosystems in states like Haryana, Manipur, and Punjab. A list of the

IMELY ORGANIZATION AND SUPPORT FOR NATIONAL GAMES 
Recommendation

Olympic Association (IOA) biennially, but that they weren’t organized between 2015 and 2022, 
partly due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Committee recommends that the Department work 
more closely with the Indian Olympic Association to ensure that the same is not repeated in the 
future. The Committee also recommends that the Department consider supporting the IOA in 
organizing the National Games annually. The Department may assist the IOA with identifying 
cities with the requisite sporting infrastructure and host the games there so as to avoid having to 
incur high expenses on capital expansion. 
(Para 5.16.1 of the 366th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
The National Games are required to be organized biennially. The primary responsibility 
for timely conduct of the National Games is that of Indian Olympic Association (IOA) and the 
concerned host state.

allotted to Goa but was later reassigned to Gujarat. However, the COVID-19 pandemic further

November 9, 2023. Furthermore, the 38th National Games were recently held from 28th January 
to 14th February, 2025 at Uttarakhand.

PREVENTION OF AGE FRAUD IN SPORTS 
Recommendation 
5. The Committee notes that another major issue that really hurts young sportspersons is 
that of over-age children competing in lower age groups. The Committee recommends that the 
Department consider solutions to this issue. 
(Para 5.6.19 of the 366th Report of the Committee) 
Action Taken 
For prevention of age fraud in sports, the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports has issued 
guidelines under the ‘National Code Against Age Fraud in Sports’ (NCAAFS), effective from 1st 
April 2010. Under NCAAFS 2010, concerned sports bodies such as National Sports Federations 
(NSFs) and Sports Authority of India (SAI) are required to get all the players in age level 
competitions medically examined at the time of registration or allowing a new athlete to 
participate in an event and issue them identity card. 
In terms of NCAAFS 2010, SAI carries out the age verification tests before admitting an 
athlete into its Sports Promotion Schemes. Likewise, NSFs are entrusted with the responsibility 
of carrying out age verification tests in accordance with the NCAAFS 2010. 
Further, the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports has put in the public domain the Draft 
National Code Against Age Fraud in Sports (NCAAFS) 2025 for inviting comments/ suggestions 
from the general public and stakeholders, as part of the consultation process. 
The Code aims to: 
 Ensure fair competition by preventing age fraud, which compromises the integrity of 
sports. 
 Implement a robust verification system for age determination through a centralized 
database. 
 Introduce strict penalties for athletes, coaches, and officials found guilty of falsifying age 
records. 
 Enhance transparency and accountability in sports governance by aligning with 
international best practices. 
 

 
26 
 
The draft NCAAFS is at consultation stage. Once finalized it will be applicable to all 
athletes, coaches, officials, administrators, and support personnel involved inrecognized National 
Sports Federations (NSFs), Sports Authority of India (SAI), Sports Control Boards managed by 
Central Government departments and Central Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) and NGOs, 
NSPOs, public/private agencies, and institutions promoting sports development.

However, in STCs providing residential facilities is the responsibility of State

enabling them to participate as day boarders under the respective schemes.

posts of High Performance Coach (HPC) too are filled up as soon as possible.

year period (i.e. 2021-22 to 2025-26). 
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee  
The Committee observes that the Scheme of Sports Fund for Pension to Meritorious 
Sportspersons is an important scheme to provide additional financial security to 
sportspersons post retirement from active sports career in the form of life-time pension.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Seventy Fifth 
Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 26) of the Department of 
Higher Education, Ministry of Education for the year 2026-27.  
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India projected under 
various Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year needs to be voted by Parliament. 
As a sequel thereto, Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand 
referred to concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close 
scrutiny thereof under Rule 270 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States (Rajya Sabha). While making scrutiny of the Demands for Grants, the

the Department of Higher Education vis-a-vis expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of 
India in the current financial year.

covered in Report number 376th of the Committee.

CHAPTER 1  
INTRODUCTION 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT OF HIGHER EDUCATION 
1.1 Higher education plays a pivotal role in the growth, stability and overall progress of a nation 
and its society. It serves as the cornerstone for the development of human capital, fostering 
intellectual advancement, innovation and socio-economic transformation. The Higher 
Educational Institutions (HEIs) act as centres of excellence where knowledge is created 
preserved and disseminated. HEIs equip students with advanced skills, critical thinking abilities 
and professional competencies necessary to meet the evolving demands of a globalized and 
technology-driven world. In essence, higher education not only drives economic growth and 
employment generation but also shapes the moral, intellectual and cultural fabric of society. It is 
in this backdrop, the Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports considered 
the Demand for Grants 2026-27 of the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education. 
1.2 The Ministry of Education (MoE) is the apex body responsible for framing and implementing 
the National Education Policy, overseeing educational programmes at all levels, and developing 
systemic educational infrastructure across the country. The Department of Higher Education is 
responsible for the overall development of the higher education sector in India, encompassing 
universities, colleges, and institutions of national importance. 
The Ministry of Education comprises of two Departments: 
(i) Department of School Education and Literacy (DoSEL); and  
(ii) Department of Higher Education (DoHE) 
1.3 Mission and Vision of the Department 
Mission: 
 Provide greater opportunities of access to higher education with equity to all eligible 
persons, particularly to vulnerable sections. 
 Expand access by supporting existing institutions, establishing new institutions, and 
supporting State Governments and non-Government Organizations/Civil Society. 
 Initiate policies and programmes for strengthening entrepreneurship, research and 
innovations and encourage institutions to engage in stretching the frontiers of knowledge. 
 Promote the quality of higher education by investing in infrastructure and faculty, 
promoting academic reforms, improving governance and institutional restructuring. 
Vision: To realize India's human resource potential to its fullest in the higher education sector 
with equity and excellence. 
1.4 Institutional Setup of the Department of Higher Education

which are given as under:

World Class Institutions 
3.2 Under the World Class Institutions scheme, the selected institutions are granted the status of 
“Institute of Eminence (IoE)”. It is a Central Sector Scheme aimed at establishing world-class 
institutions each in the public and private sector, by providing an enabling regulatory 
environment that allows them to achieve the highest levels of global excellence in teaching and 
research. The scheme grants selected institutions significant regulatory and administrative 
autonomy to facilitate their rise in global rankings. One of the major objectives of the scheme is 
that the institutions should appear in top-500 of any of the renowned global education ranking 
frameworks in a period of ten years of becoming an IoE.  
The following institutions have been granted the IoE status as of 2026: 
 Public Institutions (08): IIT-Delhi, IIT-Bombay, IIT-Madras, IIT-Kharagpur, IISc 
Bangalore, Banaras Hindu University, University of Hyderabad and University of Delhi. 
 Private Institutions (04): Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Birla Institute of 
Technology & Science, O.P. Jindal Global University and Shiv Nadar University.

comprehensive performance review of all designated IoEs should be undertaken and 
establish clearly defined, time-bound outcome benchmarks aligned with internationally 
recognised ranking parameters, along with a robust monitoring framework. The 
Committee also recommends linking future financial support to demonstrable progress in 
research output, faculty quality, internationalisation, and global academic reputation.

MERITE since its introduction despite BE allocations of Rs. 100-220 crore per year. Now 
with formal approval in August 2025 and a BE of Rs. 300 crore in 2026-27, the Committee 
is of the view that necessary steps sould be taken for timely and proper utilization of 
allocated funds in future. 

45 
 
3.46 The Committee recommends that a dedicated MERITE Project Management Unit 
(PMU) should be established with adequate technical and fiduciary staff to ensure 
compliance with World Bank IDA requirements and to accelerate project implementation 
across 350 target institutions. 
3.47 The Committee recommends that MERITE's implementation prioritise institutions in 
States with low GER in technical education and specifically in the North Eastern Region, 
ensuring that the scheme's benefits flow equitably across geographies and not merely to 
already well-resourced engineering institutions. 
3.48 The Committee recommends a comprehensive stakeholder consultation with State 
Governments and affiliated technical universities that should be completed before 
finalizing the project design, to ensure state ownership and co-investment in the project's 
outcomes. 
Malaviya Mission Teacher Training Programme (MMTTP) 
3.49 The Malaviya Mission Teacher Training Programme (MMTTP) was re-launched in 
September 2023 as a successor to the PMMMNMTT (PM's Mission for Mentoring the Nation's 
Teachers) scheme. It aims to build competencies in faculty through exposure to Indian values, 
updated knowledge and skills, and alignment with NEP 2020. The total financial outlay for FY 
2023-24 to 2025-26 is Rs. 361.59 crore.  
3.50 At present, 151 MMTTCs have been identified across the country for conducting many 
training programmes for teachers, major among them are as under: 
 Nurturing Future Leadership Program: to build faculty leadership capacity across 
different levels to create a strong pool of potential leaders for generational transition. 
NIEPA is the coordinating agency, and 33 HEIs (16 IIMs; 8 IITs; 9 Pvt. HEIs) have been 
identified as NFLP Host Institutions. 
 Capacity Building Program on Specific Learning Disabilities: to address the issue of 
learning disabilities among a set of students and to create awareness among teachers and 
to sensitize them for teaching the student with specific disabilities, including learning 
disabilities to reverse their underrepresentation.  
 Capacity Building Programme for Promoting Positive Mental Health Resilience & 
Wellbeing in HEIs: aims at sustained faculty capacity building in Higher Education 
Institutions (HEIs) by creating a platform to share best practices and collaborate with 
experts on student mental health and wellbeing. It seeks to foster an institutional 
ecosystem where the wellbeing of both students and faculty is prioritized.  
 Capacity Building Programme on Cyber Security: This 5-day onlineprogramme offers 
Basic and Intermediate cyber-security training for educators, equipping them with skills 
to promote digital security and resilience in educational institutions. The programme is 
being hosted by IIT Madras.  
 Capacity Building Programme on Artificial Intelligence: This 5-day online 
programme equips faculty and academic leaders with AI skills to enhance teaching, 
promote research, and support NEP 2020 goals. The program is being hosted by IIT 
Ropar.  

46 
 
 Capacity Building Programme on STEM: This 9-day residential programme enhances 
college faculty's STEM teaching skills, integrating innovative methods and technology to 
improve teaching, boost student performance, and foster research and inclusion. The 
program is being hosted by IIT Madras, IIT Ropar, and IISc Bangalore.

Centres of Excellence (CoEs) in Artificial Intelligence (AI) 
3.71 Artificial Intelligence is rapidly transforming sectors such as healthcare, agriculture, 
education, manufacturing, and public service delivery. Staying ahead in this domain is not 
merely a matter of technological advancement, but one of strategic importance. To establish 
India as a global leader in use of AI for public services, the Government of India announced 
establishing Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Union Budget 2023-24. 
Following the announcements, three Centres of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence were 
established at IISc Bangalore (Healthcare), IIT Kanpur (Sustainable Cities), and IIT Ropar 
(Agriculture) with total budget outlay for the three CoEs of Rs. 990 crore. These dedicated 
Centres of Excellence are necessary to create focused platforms for high-quality research, 
innovation, and skill development in this critical domain. They will enable collaboration between 
academia, industry, and government, ensuring that AI solutions are aligned with national 
developmental priorities.  
3.72 To further the vision of “Make AI in India and Make AI work for India”, a fourth CoE in AI 
for Education was announced in Budget 2025-26 with a total outlay of Rs. 500 crores and 
established at IIT Madras. This CoE aims to establish Centres of Excellence to promote 
interdisciplinary research, innovation, and capacity building in Artificial Intelligence 
applications for the education sector. It will support development of indigenous, scalable AI-
based solutions for improving teaching, learning outcomes, and educational governance. 
Separately, Rs. 17.00 cr was allotted for it in RE 2025-26 and Rs. 100.00 cr is allocated in BE 
2026-27 for this purpose.

Pradhan Mantri Vidyalaxmi Scheme (PM-VL) 
3.88 PM Vidyalaxmi (PM-VL) was approved by the Union Cabinet on 6th November 2024 as a 
new Central Sector Scheme. Its objective is to ensure that no meritorious student is denied the 
opportunity to pursue higher education due to financial constraints. The scheme facilitates 
collateral-free and guarantor-free education loans to students securing merit-based admission in 
top Quality Higher Education Institutions (QHEIs), identified through NIRF rankings. More than 
917 QHEIs have been identified, covering over 22 lakh students annually. 
Key features of the scheme are as under: 
 Collateral-free and guarantor-free education loans covering full tuition fees and course-
related expenses. 
 Credit guarantee of up to 75% of outstanding default for loans up to Rs. 7.5 lakh. 
 Interest subvention of 3% during moratorium period on loans up to Rs. 10 lakh for 
students with annual family income up to Rs. 8 lakh. 
 Total outlay: Rs. 3,600 crore for 2024-25 to 2030-31, covering an estimated 7 lakh 
students. 
 Dedicated online portal operational since 25th February 2025; all 12 Public Sector banks, 
20 leading private banks, 24 Regional Rural banks integrated on single portal. 
 Loans are made accessible through a simple, transparent, student-friendly and entirely 
digital application process; PM Vidyalaxmi Digital Rupee App (CBDC Wallet) for 

56 
 
disbursing interest subvention; the amount is credited to CBDC wallet of the beneficiary, 
then can be redeemed into bank account. 
 As on 22.01.2026, 25,385 grievances received on portal and 23,623 has been resolved. 
 Average Turn Around Time (TAT) for loan sanction ahs been reduced to less than 9 
days. 
 Simple 2-page application format (reduced from earlier 7-8 pages).

University Grants Commission (UGC) 
4.1 The University Grants Commission (UGC), established under an Act of Parliament in 1956, 
is a statutory body responsible for the coordination and maintenance of standards in universities 
throughout India. UGC provides financial assistance to eligible universities and colleges, 
promotes autonomous colleges, and advises on matters related to higher education. UGC is also 
responsible for introducing and implementing various academic reforms, including CHOICE-
Based Credit System (CBCS), Four-Year Undergraduate Programme (FYUP), academic 
autonomy, and curriculum reforms under NEP 2020. Its role and functions include coordination 
between universities; maintenance of standards; promotion of research; granting recognition to 
universities; disbursing scholarships/fellowships; framing regulations for higher education; 
promoting quality assurance through NAAC; and overseeing SWAYAM, ABC, and NIRF 
frameworks. 
4.2 Key initiatives undertaken by UGC: 
 154 Non-Technology Post-Graduate MOOCs developed for SWAYAM (2017 onwards); 
415 universities have adopted SWAYAM Credit Framework Regulations 2021; 4,55,956 
students earned credit transfers through SWAYAM (2021-2024). 
 Framework for Universities to conduct examinations for SWAYAM Courses notified 
(August 2024); 191 Universities adopted. 
 SWAYAM Outreach Workshops conducted at 8 locations (Jan-Mar 2025), with 
participation of over 7,000 stakeholders. 
 Guidelines for Incorporating Indian Knowledge in Higher Education Curricula released. 
 Mulya Pravah 2.0 introduced – focusing on human values and professional ethics. 
 Guidelines for Transforming Higher Education Institutions into Multidisciplinary 
Institutions (2022). 
 UGC (Institutions Deemed to be Universities) Regulations 2023 notified. 
 Foreign Higher Educational Institutions Regulations 2023 – facilitating branch campus 
establishment.

MISCELLANEOUS 
Research and Innovation 
5.1 Research and innovation are at the heart of any vibrant higher education system. Universities 
are not only places for teaching but also spaces where new ideas are explored, tested, and 
transformed into solutions for real-world problems. Strong research culture helps institutions 
contribute meaningfully to national priorities such as healthcare, agriculture, technology, and 
sustainable development. It also enhances academic excellence and global standing. By 
encouraging curiosity, critical thinking, and collaboration with industry, research-driven 
institutions prepare students to become innovators and leaders. In a rapidly changing world, 
continuous investment in research and innovation is essential to ensure long-term growth, 
competitiveness, and self-reliance for the nation. Key stats with regard to research and 
innovation scenario in HEIs in the country: 
 In the last 5 years, 2021 to 2025, over 1.1 Lakh patents have been filed by educational 
institutions of the country. Around 3,000 patents have been granted to centrally funded 
institutions under the Department of Higher Education during this period. 
 The IRINS (Indian Research Information Network System), which is a part of NMEICT 
has on boarded more than 1,800 higher education institutions and provided access to the 
comprehensive research profiling platform to them. The portal hosts more than 37.89 
lakh publications and approximately 2.75 lakh researcher profiles, including Assistant 
Professors, Associate Professors, and Professors. Collectively, these publications have 
garnered over 3.9 crore citations, reflecting the vast research footprint of Indian 
academia. 
 Research and innovation are central to institutional benchmarking within the Indian 
higher education ecosystem. Research & Innovation is a key criterion for Accreditation 
under National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC). Research is also among 
the five core weighted parameters of the National Institutional Ranking Framework 
(NIRF) for ranking Indian HEIs. 
 Around 6000 Institutions/Universities have established R&D Cells to catalyse 
multidisciplinary/ trans-disciplinary and translational research culture. 16,408 IICs have 
been set up in HEIs to develop a culture of research and innovation in Indian HEIs. 
 Presently 8,412 start-ups are incubated at HEIs and it is targeted to 50,000 start-ups by 
2030. 
5.2 Key initiatives taken by the Department in field of research and innovation under various 
schemes: 
 PMRF: 3,688 scholars admitted; 10,300 journal publications; 7,966 conference 
publications; 834 patents applied, 221 granted (as on 31.12.2025). 
 SPARC: 28 partner nations; research under 12 thematic areas aligned with G20 priorities; 
75.36% efficiency (DRDO evaluation, 2025). 
 STARS: Focuses on science education-research integration; allocation maintained at Rs. 
40 crore.

5.4 The Committee recognizes that strengthening research and innovation ecosystems is 
central to India in achieving a knowledge-driven economy. The Committee recommends 
that the Department, in coordination with DST, DBT, CSIR, and ANRF (Anusandhan 
National Research Foundation), develop a unified National Research Mission for higher 
education with a five-year rolling budget, clearly delineating the roles of each agency to 
avoid duplication and ensure synergistic investment. A target of increasing India's GERD 
(Gross Expenditure on R&D) from 0.64% of GDP to at least 1.5% of GDP by 2030 should 
be embedded in this Mission. 
5.5 IIT data shows 9,393 patents applied and 5,733 granted between 2019 and 2025, but 
commercialization of these patents remains limited. The Committee is of the view that a 
Technology Transfer and Commercialization Office be established as a central facilitation 
body, interfacing with the private sector, DPIIT, and Start-up India may be established, to 
convert publicly-funded research into market-ready products and processes. 
5.6 While CFIs like IITs and IISc have world-class research infrastructure, State 
universities - which account for over 80% of enrolled students - have negligible research 
capacity. The Committee recommends that a dedicated 'State University Research 
Enhancement Fund' under PM-USHA with an annual outlay of at least Rs. 500 crore to 
develop Research and Innovation Clusters should be established at State universities, with 
matching contributions from State Governments. 
5.7 Consistent with NEP 2020's vision of multidisciplinarity, the Committee recommends 
that as per UGC notified guidelines Multi-Disciplinary Research Centres in every Central 
University should be established by 2027, covering at least three convergence areas such as 
AI and healthcare, sustainability and urban planning, or materials science and agriculture 
to facilitate establishing seed centres. 
5.8 The Committee notes that the Department does not currently publish a consolidated 
research output report mapping budget allocations to publications, patents, and citations 
across schemes. The Committee recommends that the Department should introduce an 
Annual Research Outcomes Report covering PMRF, SPARC, STARS, CoE-AI, MERITE, 
and all research-linked schemes, enabling Parliament and the public to assess the return on 
India's research investment in higher education.

5.13 The Committee emphasizes that a well-structured scholarship and fellowship 
ecosystem is essential to ensure that no deserving student is denied access to higher 
education due to financial constraints. To facilitate this, the Department currently operates 
multiple scholarship schemes — CSSS, SSS-JKL, CSIS, PMRF, UGC-JRF/SRF, NET-JRF, 

71 
 
and PM Vidyalaxmi — through different portals with separate application processes. The 
Committee recommends that a Single Integrated Scholarship Portal under the National 
Scholarship Portal (NSP) 2.0 should be developed, where a student can apply for all eligible 
schemes simultaneously through a single form and single KYC process, with automated 
eligibility matching and DBT disbursement. 
5.14 The Central Sector Scholarship Scheme (CSSS) provides Rs. 12,000 per annum for the 
first three years, a rate that has remained static for several years despite rising cost of 
education. Similarly, UGC fellowship stipends for PhD scholars were last revised in 2019. 
The Committee recommends an immediate upward revision of all scholarship and 
fellowship amounts - at minimum linked to CPI inflation - and thereafter indexed 
automatically every three years. 
5.15 Prestigious fellowships like PMRF are limited to scholars at IITs, IISc, and a select list 
of institutions. The Committee recommends introduction of a dedicated Post-Doctoral 
Fellowship Scheme for researchers at accredited State universities and government 
colleges, with at least 2,000 fellowships per year at an enhanced stipend of Rs. 75,000 -
85,000 per month, to stimulate a research culture beyond the elite institutions. 
5.16 The Committee notes that UGC fellowship data shows year-on-year increase in SC, 
ST, and OBC fellowship holders; however, the proportion relative to enrolled population in 
these categories remains unclear. The Committee recommends that the Department should 
conduct a comprehensive gap analysis - mapping the number of eligible 
SC/ST/OBC/PwD/Minority students enrolled in PhD programmes against the number 
actually receiving fellowships - and take corrective action to bridge the gap at the earliest.

5.19 The Committee notes that while overall STEM enrolment is growing, female 
participation in engineering and technology courses remains disproportionately low (42.6% 
as per AISHE 2021-22). The Committee is of the view that AICTE and UGC should jointly 
develop Gender Parity in STEM Action Plan with institution-specific targets for female 
enrolment and offer scholarships exclusively for women in STEM at postgraduate and 
doctoral levels in all HEIs. 
5.20 Many government degree colleges and State university-affiliated colleges lack 
functional STEM laboratories, forcing students to learn from textbooks alone. The 
Committee recommends that PM-USHA's Phase 3 should prioritise laboratory 
modernisation and equipment grants for STEM disciplines, with a minimum of Rs. 50 lakh 
per institution for science lab upgradation and Rs. 1 crore for engineering workshops, 
covering at least10% of HEIs. 
5.21 AICTE's Model Curriculum in AI, Data Science, and Robotics is a commendable step; 
however, adoption across the 10,000+ AICTE-approved institutions is limited. The 
Committee recommends that AICTE mandate updated STEM curriculum adoption as a 
condition for annual approval renewal, with a three-year implementation timeline. Faculty 
retraining through MMTTP should be specifically aligned with the updated STEM 
content. 
5.22 The Committee emphasizes that India's STEM innovation potential is constrained by 
geographical concentration of research in metropolitan and Tier-1 city institutions. The 
Committee recommends a STEM Research Cluster programme to establish 50 STEM 
Research Clusters at government institutions in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities over a period of 
five years, with seed funding of Rs. 5-10 crore each under a dedicated scheme, focusing on 
applied research relevant to local industries, agricultural and environmental challenges. 
5.23 Of India's 45,000+ colleges, only a fraction has implemented SWAYAM credit transfer 
despite 415 universities adopting the framework. The Committee recommends that UGC 

73 
 
should take necessary steps mandating all affiliated colleges to allow students to earn at 
least 20% of their total academic credits through SWAYAM courses, with a phased 
implementation timeline starting from academic year 2026-27. Non-compliance should be 
flagged during NAAC accreditation assessment. 
5.24 The Committee appreciates SWAYAM Plus, with 89 industry partners and 4.8 lakh 
enrolments, which has demonstrated strong industry appetite for skilling through the 
MOOC model. The Committee recommends that SWAYAM Plus should target more  
industry partners and enrolments, with specific campaigns in MSME and manufacturing 
sectors where skilling gaps are acute. Completion certificates from SWAYAM Plus should 
be recognised under the National Credit Framework (NCrF). 
5.25 The Committee observes that despite India's linguistic diversity, the majority of 
SWAYAM courses are in English or Hindi while a significant proportion of India's student 
population learns best in their mother tongue. The Committee recommends that by 2027-
28, at least 500 SWAYAM courses be made available in each of the 22 Scheduled 
Languages, with dedicated funding for translation, dubbing, and regional language content 
creation, and involvement of regional language universities and State governments in 
content development.

5.33 The Committee notes the recent policy reforms enabling reputed foreign universities 
to establish campuses in India. While recognising the potential benefits in terms of global 
exposure and academic collaboration, the Committee underscores the need for robust 
regulatory oversight. It recommends that clear safeguards be instituted to ensure that such 
institutions reinvest a reasonable portion of their surplus within India. The Committee 
further is of the view that course curricula maintain an appropriate balance between global 
standards and Indian academic, cultural, and developmental contexts. Therefore, periodic

1. The Committee notes with appreciation the 11.28% increase in BE 2026-27 (Rs. 
55,727.22 crore) over BE 2025-26. However, it observes that actual expenditure in 2024-
25 (Rs. 45,576.52 crore) fell short of the BE by nearly Rs. 4,500 crore. The Committee is 
of the view that a robust quarterly expenditure monitoring mechanism should be 
instituted by the Department to ensure full utilization of allocated funds for overall 
development of Higher Education ecosystem and prevent lapse of public resources. 
(para 2.12) 
 
2. India's total public expenditure, both Centre and States, on education as a 
percentage of GDP stood at 4.06% (2022-23), which is significantly below the NEP 2020 
target of 6% of GDP. The Committee recommends that the Government should take 
concrete, time-bound steps to progressively increase the education budget, with a clear 
roadmap to achieve at least the 6% target by 2030. 
(para 2.13) 
 
3. The Committee is of the view that the Department should prepare and submit an 
annual Performance Budget with scheme-wise KPI linkage to allocations, and actual 
achievement against targets for all major schemes under the Department for its

10.27 crore in BE 2025-26 to Rs. 2.68 crore in BE 2026-27) and recommends a five-year 
Capital Investment Plan with direct capital allocation from BE 2027-28. 
(para 2.15)

regarding the issue of delayed submission of Utilisation Certificates by 
grantees/institutions and is of the view that it needs to be addressed by putting in place a 
mechanism that makes it possible to fix accountability of the officers concerned. The 
Committee recommends that the reasons given by grantees/institutions in response to 
delay in submission also needs to be properly scrutinized and verified. The Committee 
also recommends that the Department should take proactive steps for highlighting the 
status of each grantee/institution and pendency of Utilisation Certificates against it on a

states that rush to expenditure particularly in the closing months of financial year shall 
be regarded as a breach of financial propriety and shall be avoided. As per their 
guidelines, the last quarter expenditure must be limited to actual procurement of goods 
and services and reimbursement of expenditure already occurred. Ministry of Finance's 
instructions seeks to restrict last quarter expenditure to 33 per cent ceiling and last 
month (March) expenditure to 15 per cent ceiling.

2025-26 and Rule 56(3) of General Financial Rules (GFR), Ministry of Finance, the
