REPORT

1. The Department of Culture plays a vital role in the promotion and dissemination of
art and culture. The aim of the Department is to develop ways and means for instilling basic
values and perceptions in the minds of people, particularly the young. The Department also
undertakes the programme of preservation, encouragement and dissemination of various
manifestations of creative activity, both past and present. The Department is engaged in
excavation, conservation and promotion of ancient monuments and historic sites; administra-
tion of libraries, museums and institutions of anthropology; collection, preservation and
ethnology of national character; catering to institutions and organisations in the areas of
Buddhist and Tibetan Studies; promoting literary, visual and performing arts; observing
centenaries and anniversaries of important personalities and entering into cultural agree-
ments with foreign countries.

1.1 The Department carries out its various programmes through two attached offices,
six subordinate offices and 26 autonomous organisations. The Department of Culture has
been allocated Rs. 203.23 crores which includes 113.76 crores as Plan component and 89.47
crores as non-Plan component. The allocation of funds during the Eighth Five Year Plan to
Department of Culture was Rs. 460 crores which is only 0.19% of the total Plan outlay. The
Committee strongly feels the necessity of increasing the allocation.

1.2 The Revised Estimates (RE) for 1995-96 for the Department of Culture was Rs.
211.27 crores which has been slashed down to Rs. 203.23 crores in the Budget Estimates of
1996-97. Explaining its justification the Department answered the RE of 1995-96 included a
provision of one time grant of Rs. 10 crores to National Gandhi Museum on the occasion of
the 125th Birth Anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, but the BE for 1996-97 do not include any
such special provision and, hence, the decrease of Rs. 8.04 crores. For the year 1996-97, the
‘Department had asked for an enhanced allocation of Rs. 273.40 crores under Plan
allocation. However, the Planning Commission after assuring an allocation of Rs. 237 crores,
actually approved a Plan outlay of Rs. 113.76 crores only. The Committee is of the view that
the Planning Commission has not taken a realistic view of the conservation of our cultural
heritage, particularly when the nation is going to celebrate its 50th year of Independence.
The Committee recommends allocation of required amount at the RE stage.

1.3 The Committee, in its Tenth and Eighteenth Reports recomended for setting up of
a National Cultural Fund. The Committee was given to understand that a corpus fund with
the Government contribution of Rs. 19.5 crores has been created. On this the Department
clarified that due to resource crunch the amount from Government side was reduced to 19.5
crores from Rs. 100 crores as proposed originally. The fund has, however, not so far been
set up. Clarifying this the Department informed the Committee that the efforts to set up the
fund are maturing. The proposals, as finalised, providing for the setting up of the Fund and
the Scheme to administer it, stand referred to the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Law and
Justice and Planning Commission for concurrence. The Committee strongly recommends that
the Department should vigorously pursue the matter with them for getting it cleared at the
earliest. The Committee desires that the UNESCO should also be approached for additional
funding.


ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA, NEW DELHI

2. The Archaeological Survey of India was set up in 1861. Conservation, preservation
and maintenance of the centrally protected monuments and sites is the prime task of this
organisation. At present, it has 3562 centrally protected monuments, declared to be of
national importance, with more than 5000 structures

2.1 The BE for 1996-97 is Rs. 52.35 crores as against Rs. 50.85 crores in the RE for the
year 1995-96. Commenting on the increase in the budget provision, the Department of
Culture has stated that even this amount falls short of the requirements. It is also a cause for
concern that if sufficient funds are not provided in the Revised Estimate 1996-97, it may be
difficult even to disburse the salary and allowances of the employees besides meeting office
expenses during the current financial year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
sufficient allocation should be made to the ASI, at RE stage.

2.2 The Committee had earlier recommended to expand the network of ASI and to
increase the staff strength. The Department had formed a Committee with the Joint
Director, SIU, Ministry of Finance to assess actual requirement of the staff through the spot
inspection. But this Committee is yet to visit any circle. The Committee feels that there is
virtually no progress in this respect and there is an urgent need for filling up required
number of vacancies at the earlies:.

2.3 The Committee is concerned to note that Taj Mahal remains closed on Monday and
the entry fee for it after 4 P.M. onwards has been increased to Rs. 100/. Regarding entry
fee for the Taj Mahal, the Secretary stated that at present, the Archaeological Survey of
India has been charging only 50 paise per person. However, with effect from Ist September,
1996, the entry fee for Taj Mahal and some other major monuments will be raised to Rs. 5
per person; in respect of comparatively less important monuments, the entry fee was being
revised to Rs. 2 per person, he added. For the purpose of maintenance, the Taj is also being
closed on Mondays. As regards the levy of Rs. 100 for entering the Taj before 9 A.M. and
after 4.00 P.M., Secretary (Culture) clarified that this had been done by the Agra
Development Authority and that State Government is separately apprising the Supreme
Court as to how this money is being utilised for development of Taj Mahal and Agra. The
Committee, however, desires that the Department should take up the matter with the State
Government of U.P. to reduce the levy of Rs. 100 to a reasonable limit.

NATIONAL MUSEUM

3. The Committee is constrained to observe that during the transit of exhibits for
holding exhibitions abroad and also during the course of the exhibitions there, sufficient
protection to art pieces is not taken care of due to which several exhibits are damaged. In its
reply the Department stated that necessary steps are taken for protecting the art objects in
accordance with the guidelines. The Committee feels that instead of original documents,
replicas may be sent in the exhibitions including those meant to be placed at the festivals
abroad. This would ensure the safety and security of the precious and rare exhibits.
INDIAN MUSEUM, CALCUTTA

4. The Indian Museum, established in 1814, is the oldest and the largest institution of
its kind in the country. It houses unique treasures of Indian and foreign art, representing
centuries of cultural ethos and traditions.

4.1 The Indian Museum, Calcutta was allocated Rs. 2 crores on Plan side and Rs. 1.19
crores on non-Plan side in the BE of 1996-97, which remained same as compared to RE of
1995-96. It may be increased at RE stage.


4.2. The Committee has observed that five organisations namely. Botanical, Zoological,
Geological, Anthropological and Archaeological Survey of India are occuping space in the
Indian Museum, Calcutta. The Department stated that there was no possibility of vacating
the space by these organisations in the near future. The Committee, however, desires that
the matter may be pursued vigorously.

SALARJUNG MUSEUM, HYDERABAD

5. It was brought to the notice of the Committee that some important materials and
jewellaries were missing from the Salarjung Museum. The Committee is of the view that
sufficient security measures are not taken by the Museum and Committee recommends that
enough security measures may be taken immediately.

5.1 The Salarjung Museum has undertaken the construction of two additional wings i.e.
Far Eastern Gallery and European Gallary which were supposed to be completed by 31st
May, 1996 and 15th July, 1996, respectively. The Committee is constrained to note that the
construction work has not yet been completed by the scheduled dates. The National Building
Construction Corporation (NBCC) which is doing the construction job there has sought
extention upto 31st December, 1996. The Committee hopes that the construction would be
completed at least by the revised date.

NATIONAL COUNCIL OF SCIENCE MUSEUMS, CALCUTTA

6. The Committee in its 18th Report had recommended for taking necessary steps to
involve ‘Nagarpalikas and Panchayats’ in the NCSM’s new programme for setting up small
size low capital intensive school science centres in underpriviledged schools in rural areas.
The Department has stated that the Nagarapalikas and Panchayats would henceforth be
involved in these activities. The Committee, however, feels that there is no progress in this
regard and concrete steps are required to be taken immediately.

SCHEME FOR PROMOTION AND STRENGTHENING OF REGIONAL AND LOCAL
MUSEUMS

7. The aim of this scheme is to enable establishment of Regional Museums in the
country. The Budgetary provision made during the last year was Rs. 1 crore which remained
the same in the BE for 1996-97. The Committee in its 18th report had recommended that
steps be taken to involve Panchayats and Nagarpalikas in this scheme. The Department
stated in its reply that at the district level, Panchayats and Nagarpalikus are proposed to be
included. The Committee feels that no concrete steps have so far been taken. Hence the
Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that necessary steps should be taken to
involve the Panchayats and Nagarpalikas in it.

NATIONAL RESEARCH LABORATORY FOR CONSERVATION OF CULTURAI
PROPERTY, LUCKNOW

8. This institute is a subordinate office of the Department of Culture established in 1976
engaged in the conservation of cultural property including monuments and development of
conservation techniques through short-term and long-term research projects. The budgetary
provision for the institution for the year 1996-97 on the Plan side is Rs. 1.10 crores and on
the non-Plan side Rs. 0.55 crores which may be further increased at RE stage.

8.1 The Committee was given to understand that the historical monuments of great
national importance in Lucknow like Imambara, Mosques and other Maqbaras in the -
adjoining areas are in a depleting stage in the absence of proper care and upkeep. Many of
these monuments have their great historical past which needs to be preserved. The
Committee was given to understand that the President of Iran, during his visit to Lucknow,
last year had announed a grant of Rs. 1 crore exclusively for the upkeep and maintenance of
these historical monuments and to preserve the cultural heritage of this great city of


4

Lucknow. Unfortunately, this money has not reached the place yet, with the result that
these monuments are further decaying. The Committee desires that the position with regard
to this external aid may be checked up and the Ministry of Finance be approached for
making budgetary provisions for this purpose at the RE stage. The Government has no right
to withhold any such grant received from an external agency meant for the preservation and
maintenance of historical monuments of great national importance. The amount should be
utilised for the purpose for which it has been given to the Government of India by the
Iranian Government.

8.2 The Committee was also given to understand that an amount of Rs. 11 to Rs. 12
crores was received by Hussainabad Trust for the maintenance, upkeep and preservation of
very good and rare pieces of architecture in this area. There are a number of monuments of
historical importance but they have not so far been declared as monuments of national
importance. These pieces .f rare art and architecture need to be protected and preserved
with the Government's intervention. The residency is also reported to be in very bad shape.
This residency was the centre of attraction during the freedom struggle. Earlier there used to
be a light and sound show which has since been closed. The Committee being distressed to
hear the sad state of affairs, strongly recommends that every effort should be made to
preserve the cultural heritage of these monuments and the grant of Rs. one crore received
from the President of Iran should be utilised for this purpose without any delay.

ANTHROPOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA

9. The allocation in the RE for 1995-96 on its Plan side was Rs. 1.60 crores, which has
been reduced to Rs. 0.98 crores in 1996-97 BE. Commenting on this reduction, the
Department stated that total allocation for the Eighth Five Year Plan for Anthropological
Survey of India was Rs. 6.00 crores out of which Rs. 5.02 crores were already allocated
during the previous 4 years of the Eighth Five Year Plan. Hence it was restricted to Rs. 0.98
crores only for 1996-97. The Committee feels that the amount allocated for this year is too
limited and it would certainly hamper the progress of the working of Anthropological Survey
of India. The Committee feels that there is a need for rational allocations to be made each
year. Anthropoligcal Survey of India has undertaken a project called “People of India”
under which 43 volumes are expected to be brought out. However, only 8 National volumes
and 14 States volumes have been brought out so far. The Committee recommends that the
remaining volumes also should be completed at the earliest. The reduction in the allocation
is also likely to hamper the progress of this project. The Committee, therefore, desires that
the required funds may be restored at the RE stage.

LIBRARIES

10. Outlay for Libraries was Rs. 17.16 crores in the RE for 1995-96, Where as BE of
1996-97 is only Rs. 14.29 crores. The Department stated that the RE for the year 1995-96
included the amount of Rs. 3 crores for the “School-cum-Village Libraries”. The scheme was
not approved by the Finance Ministry. Hence there was no allocation for this scheme
resulting in reduced allocation in 1996-97, the Department added. The Scheme was not
approved by the Ministry of Finance during 1995-96. The matter was referred to the
Planning Commission for evaluation of the existing schemes on Library Services with special
reference to the utility of the scheme of School-cum-Village Libraries. The evaluation is
being processed by the Planning Commission, and the matter is being actively persued, the
Department added. The Committee desires that an early decision is required to be taken in
the matter.

10.1 The Committee in its 18th Report recommended to spread the network of libraries


5

with computer facilities particularly in small towns. The Department stated that Raja Ram-
Mohan Roy Library Foundation had organised a conference of State Library Planning
Convenors in August, 1995 which recommended the networking of Libraries to the District
level Report of the working group on Libraries and Informatics which recommended that all
Libraries should be linked through networks and that the INFLIBNET should be made fully
operational, is under consideration, the Department added. The Committee recommends that a
final view should be taken in the matter at the earliest.

KHUDA BAKSH ORIENTAL PUBLIC LIBRARY, PATNA

10.2 Khuda Baksh Oriental Public Library, Patna is an institution of national importance
which maintains more than 18,000 manuscripts, 95,000 old and rare printed books and over 200
original paintings of Mughal, Rajput, Iranian and Turkish Schools. This Library has instituted a
Khuda Baksh Award to recognise the original creative work done in related fields. The
Committee has been given to understand that the condition of this library is in a bad shape The
preservation and upkeep of manuscripts in it is not properly done. The Committee recommends
that a thorough study be made on the functioning of this library and proper upkeep and
preservation of manuscripts be ensured.

THANJAVUR MAHARAJA SERFOJI’S SARASVATI MAHAL LIBRARY THANJAVUR

10.3 The Thanjavur Maharaja Serfoji’s Sarasvati Mahal Library, is one of the few medieval
libraries that exist in the world, It symbolises a priceless repository of culture and time defying
treasure house of knowledge, built up by the successive dynasties of Nayaks and Marathas of
Thanjavur. The library embodies rich and rare collection of manuscripts on all the features of
art, culture and literature. The Committee has noted the fact that valuable palm leaf
manuscripts containing important information about Siddha medicines are available here. The
Committee recommends that the Department of Culture may take necessary steps to publish
the material in a suitable manner.

NATIONAL LIBRARY, CALCUTTA

11. The Committee is of the view that much attention is not being given on the preservation
work of the Library. The Committee is constrained to note that the Library is starved of funds.
There is also scarcity of staff. The Secretary accepted that inadequate staff, due to 10%
compulsory cut in recruitment, has adversely affected not only the governance but also the
preservation of documents in the Library. The Committee was informed that the recuitment
rules for filling up various posts. in the National Library has since been finalised based on
chottopadhyay Committee’s recommendation and the vacant posts would be filled up shortly.
The Committee is deeply anguished to observe that a Microfilming Equipment bought in
1993-94 has not yet been used due to paucity of staff. The Committee feels that the staff
problem brooks no delay and should be solved immediately, Required funds may be released at

RE stage.
RAJA RAMMOHAN ROY LIBRARY

12. The Committee had earlier recommended for appointment of an Enquiry Committee to
look into the purchasing methodology of this library. The Department informed that the
Enquiry Committee had submitted its report. However, the present methodology of purchase of
books has not been adversely commented upon by this enquiry Committee, the Department
added. The Committee, however, desires that a regular monitoring should be kept on the
activities of this Library.

12.1 The Enquiry Committee has also recommended to spread the Library Movement to
Village Level. The Committee is of the view that this should be expedited immediately.


DELHI PUBLIC LIBRARY

13. The Committee had earlier recommended to spread the network of the Delhi Public
Library in the slum and under-developed areas. The Department stated that the DPL has
not taken up the construction of Library building in Raja Garden, Janak Puri, R.K. Puram,
Patparganj and Ashok Vihar due to non-availability of funds. The M.C.D. and N.D.M.C
had been approached by the authorities of the DPL since 1992 for allotment of suitable
accommodation for setting up libraries in slum and under-developed areas. The Committee
is, however, constrained to note that though the matter has been vigorously pursued by the
then Director and the administration of the DPL, no success has been achieved in this
direction so far. The present authorities of DPL will be meeting the Chief Minister of Delhi
shortly, to discuss the proposals and prospects of DPL, the Department added. The
Committee feels that there is an urgent need to spread the library facilities in the slum and
under developed areas of Delhi. The required funds and accommodation should be made

available at the earliest.

AKADEMIES

14. The Sahitya Akademi, Lalit kala Akademi and Sangeet Natak Akademi have been
allocated in the plan side Rs. 2.75 crores. Rs. 1.70 crores and Rs. 3.10 crores respectively,
Only in case of Sahitya Akademi Rs. 0.25 crores have been increased in the BE of 1996-97
as compared to RE of 1995-96. The Committee feels that this meagre amount is inadequate
for the Akademies. Hence the Committee is of the view that adequate funds may be
allocated. at RE stage.

14.1 The Committee expresses its concern over the misuse of funds and autonomy in the
Lalit Kala Akademi. They have also not implemented the recommendations made by the
Haksar Committee. However, in view of the serious nature of the alleged irregularities in
this Akademi, it has been decided to institute two enquiries into the recent happenings at
Lalit Kala Akademi; one of the equiries will be conducted by Chief Accounts Officer of the
Department and the other from the Vigilance angle by a Director of the Department, the
Secretary added. The Committee recommends that the enquiries may be completed at the
earliest and necessary action taken thereon.

CENTRE FOR CULTURAL RESOURCE AND TRAINING (CCRT)

15. The allocation made on the plan side for 1996-97 is Rs. 3.10 crores and on non-plan
side Rs. 0.84 crores. The Committee in its 18th Report had recommended for opening of
new CCRTs. The Department stated that due to inadequate resources, opening new CCRTs
will be a difficult proposition. The Committee desires that adequate allocations be made for
this purpose. The Department should chalk out a plan for expansion and seek for additional

funds.
ZONAL CULTURAL CENTRES (ZCC)

15.1° The main purpose is to emphasise the Cultural Linkages that extend beyond
territorial and linguistic boundaries. These centres reflect not only the forms and styles of
different States by which they stand but also represent jointly the composite culture of the
country. The Budget allocation for it is Rs. 2.10 crores which was at the same level last year
also. This scheme is in need of funds and the required funds may be given at RE stage. The
Committee was informed by the Department that a Review Committee had been set up
under that Chairmanship of Dr. U.R. Ananthamurthy to review the functioning of the Zonal
Cultural Centres (ZCC) and its report was submitted in January, 1996. The report has been


7

sent to Centres, Secretaries of the Academies and the State Governments falling under the
jurisdiction of respective Zonal Cultural Centres. The comments from many agencies are still
awaited, the Department added. The Committee desires that the Dej.rtment should pursue
the matter vigorously with all agencies for sending their comments at the earliest as all is not
well in the functioning of Zonal Cultural Centres. After the comments are received, the
Department should take action without much loss of time.

ASSISTANCE TO DANCE, DRAMA AND THEATRE ENSEMBLES

15.2 Under this scheme assistance in the form of salary grant, production grant is given to
well established voluntary cultural organisations for promoting the cultural heritage of the
country. The allocation for 1996-97 on the Plan side is Rs. 2.00 crores and non-plan side is
Rs. 0.40 crores. The scheme is suffering from the under-utilisation of funds. During 1993-94
and 1994-95 the funds could not be utilised fully. The Committee strongly recommends that
full utilisation of the funds should be ensured. Lucknow is a large treasure house of art and
culture; particularly Puppet Dances (Kathputli Dance) Marathi Natya Sangeet in
Maharashtra is culturally a rich art form. However, all such art forms are not getting any
kind of encouragement. They need immediate attention for revival.

DISEMINATION OF TRIBAL, FOLK ART AND CULTURE

15.3 The Scheme provides for financial assistance to voluntary cultural organisations,
institutions and individuals both tribal and non-tribal for undertaking small projects of about
a year’s duration on preservation, development and dissemination, of tribal/folk arts and
culture. The Committee feels that special attention needs to be paid for the dissemination of
Tribal Folk Art and Cultural especially in the tribal areas of Orissa. Madhya Pradesh,
Andhra Pradesh and other places. There is a provision for constructing a Centre for
promotion of tribal folk arts and Culture in Hyderabad. But there is no significant
concentration of tribal people in and around Hyderabad. Tribals are located in
Vizianagaram, Srikakulam and Koraput. The Committee, therefore feels that a Tribal
Centre should be appropriately set up in those areas where there is concentration of tribal
population. One finds different kinds of cultural patterns among the tribals of Andhra
Pradesh and Orissa. Steps should be taken to preserve and encourage their culture and they
should be integrated with the rest of the population and the dominant culture.

FESTIVAL OF INDIA

>

15.4 The Government of India has organised festivals of India in United Kingdom, USA,
France, CIS (Former USSR), Sweden, Germany, China and Thailand. These festivals have
been quite successful in carrying the message of the country across the seas and have served
as vehicles for disseminating Indian Culture abroad. The allocation for 1996-97 is Rs. 2.20
crores which is at the same level as that of the last year. The Committee feels that proper
utilisation of money needs to be ensured. The Committee also desires that allocation may be
suitably increased. It has come to the notice of the Committee that various exhibits of
bronze and silver are taken abroad in their original forms for Festivals of India. It has also
come to notice of the Committee that the idols of ancient temples are also carried for the
exhibition purpose in the Festivals stating that those idols are not worshipped in the temples
and, therefore have no sacred value. The Committee, however feels that, even though they
do not have sacred value, but they have the archive value and they should not be allowed to
-be carried abroad in original.


SCHEME FOR SETTING UP MUL¥I-PURPOSE CULTURE COMPLEXES

15.5 The objective of the scheme is to provide financial assistance to autonomous bodies set
up by the State Governments for establishment of cultural complexes for improving the
quality of life among youth and students and making them sensitive to what is aesthetically
and morally good in our society. These are also expected to expose the youth to the finest
forms of creative expression and to foster coordinated activities in the States in different
cultural fields, such as music, drama, dance, literature, fine arts, etc. The Budgetary allocation
for the year 1996-97 has been reduced to Rs. 1.50 crores as compared to Rs. 2.00 crores last
year. the Committee desires that the scheme needs to be restored the required funds. The
Committee feels that there should be one Multi-Purpose Centre at each block level under the
roof of which all the activities of human resource development such as cultural, sports,
education, health could be converged. The Committee recommends that a proposal may be
worked out in this direction in tendem with all other Departments of the Ministry.

MEMORIALS AND CENTENARIES

16. The Committee has been given to understand that the former Prime Minister had
announced a grant of Rs. 6.25 crores for Netaji Research Bureau which is situated in the
ancestral house of Netaji. The present Prime Minister also visited Netaji Bhavan and
reiterated that the grant will be given to the Bureau for development and to keep the
archieves in perfect condition. It was a grant of Rs. 12 crores, half of which was to be released
immediately. This is also going to be the Centenary Year of Netaji. The Committee, however,
is constrained to note that nothing has been done so far by the Department in this regard. The
Museum has not received any grant so far. The Committee was astonished to note that the
Secretary, Department of Culture was not aware of the announcements made by the former
and the present Prime Minister of India in this regard. The Committee strongly recommends
that the matter may be taken up with the Ministry of Finance and Prime Minister’s Office
immediately for an early release of the grant without any more delay.

16.1 The Government of India has decided to celebrate birth centenaries of Shri V.K.
Krishna Menon, Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose, Shri Morarji Desai, centenary of Enlighten-
ment of Bhagwan Ramana Maharishi and comemoration of 50 years of India’s Independence.
The Committee observes that the centenaries of National Leaders like Rana Pratap, Mirza
Ghalib Acharya Vinoba Bhave and Surya Kant Nirala and 500 years of Tulsi Das may also be
included in the list.

50TH YEAR OF INDIA’S INDEPENDENCE

16.2 The Committee is glad to note that the Nation will be celebrating its 50th Year of
Independence soon. The Committee has been informed that the Government has decided to
celebrate the occasion in a befitting manner from 15th August, 1997 to 15th August, 1998. The
Department of Culture has been designated as the nodal agency for it. It was also decided to
constitute a National Committee under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister, an
Implementation Committee under the Chairmanship of the Minister of Human Resource
Development and a Cabinet Committee under the Chairmanship of the Home Minister, the
Department added. The Committee desires that this historic occasion should be celebrated in
a befitting manner. It is indeed a pride occasion for the country. The occasion should also be
taken as an opportunity for the cultural renaissance. Our rich cultural heritage, moral values
and ethos should be reflected in the celebrations. The Department should gear itself up and
rise to the occasion to celebrate this great national event in a grand and befitting manner.


CULTURAL AGREEMENTS AND CULTUKAL EXCHANGE PROGRAMME

17. The allocation made for the scheme during 1996-97 is Rs. 0.365 crores. The
Committee has noted that at present the Government of India has cultural agreements with
98 countries, out of which specific biennial / triennial cultural exchange programme have
been entered into with 70 countries. The Committee feels that allocation is not sufficient and
needs to be suitably increased.

INDIRA GANDHI NATIONAL CENTRE FOR ARTS, NEW DELHI

18. The centre was set up in 1987. A sum of Rs. 25 crores was released to the centre as
the initial corpus fund with the stipulation that the centre would run on the interest accruing
from the investment. During the Eighth Plan an additional corpus fund of Rs. 25 crores was
approved. The allocation for 1996-97 is the same, both on Plan side and Non-Plan side, as
that of 1994-95 i.e. Rs. 20 crores on Plan side and Rs. 2 lakhs on Non-Plan side. The
Committee is of the view that the centre is being allotted substantial budgetary allocations
and its activities must commensurate with the sanctioned funds.

NATIONAL POLICY ON CULTURE

19. The Committee had earlier considered the Approach Paper on the National Policy
on Culture and after a detailed and indepth study of the varied aspects of Indian cultural
scene in its 12th Report, recommended early drafting of the final document on National
Policy on Culture.

19.1 The Committee is not happy with the inordinate delay in drafting the National
Policy on Culture. The Secretary informed that the draft of National Cultural Policy was
now ready and was being processed for obtaining approval of the Cabinet. Drafting the
document had not been an easy task, given the complexity of the issues involved, he added.
The Committee is not happy with the reply and recommends early finalisation of the
National Policy on Culture.

19.2 The Secretary (Culture) also informed that the Department of Culture proposed to
create five organised services i.e. :

(a) Indian Archaeological Service;

(b) Indian Archival Service;

(०) Indian Museums. and Arts Service;
(d) Indian Anthropological Service; and
(e) Indian Library Service.

With the constitution of these services, the gap in the demand and supply of trained
professionals in the aforementioned field will be automatically filled up and the prestigious
cultural organisations of the country will have culture managers of highest calibre.
Visualising the necessity of such professionally specialised services, the Committee recom-
mends for finalisation of the proposal.

19.3 The Committee also observes that in the face of cultural invasion by the West,
through electronic media, India has to bring its voice through its great cultural heritage.
Gandhian Philosophy with its voice for non-violence and peace now stands symbiotically


10

| the voice of UNESCO which focusses its attention on “From Culture of War to Culture
of Peace’. In this respect not only is there a need for Preservation of culture but also a need
for ‘Cultural Renaissance’. In this 50th year of Independence, culture should be the centre
of gravity for India’s progress.

REPORT

1, The most pressing problem faced to-day by the country is the rapid growth of
population. The Population of India has risen from 342 million in 1947 to 846.3 million in
1991 and to an estimated 950 million by the end of 1995. The rapid increase in population
has serious implications on the over all socio-economic development of the country.
Visualising this fact the Government of India was the first national Government in the world
to adopt Family Planning Programme on a national basis in 1951. The objective was to
reduce the birth rate and to stabilise the population at a level consistent with the
requirements of the development of the nation.

1.1 While making the presentation, about the activities and achievements of the
Department, the Secretary informed the Committee that from the year 1986, witu the
introduction of universal Immunisation programme, the component of mother and child
health has became very prominent. The Secretary also stated that now the overall
programme is not only on population stabilisation but also on mother and child health.

1.2 The Secretary also informed the Committee that from Ist April, 1996 the approach
towards Family Welfare Programme has been decentralised. Based on this approach, the
health centres in the country have been asked to identify the needs of the population and to
make an assessment of the population residing in the primary health centre areas. The
Secretary further elaborated that while identifying the needs of the population these
instructions will not be carried out in the first year. For the instructions to be carried out
effectively consultations have to be made with the Gram Pardhans, Primary School teachers,
Non-Governmental Organisations who are working in the field level, he added.

1.3 The Secretary also informed the Committee that there should be a convergence of
the field workers of the adult education, a movement of the primary school teachers, the
Anganwadi workers who are in charge of I.C.D.S projects and Auxiliary Nurse Midwives
(ANM) both male and female, so that the programme can be carried out in a better way.

1.4 The Committee agrees that there should be a convergence of the field workers of
the adult education, a movement of the primary school teacl.ers, Anganwadi workers and
auxiliary mid-wife both male and female, so as to ensure the success of the Family Welfare
Programme. The Committee is also of the view that there is a close co-relation between girl
education and small family. The Committee has also noted that the main reason for the
success of Family Welfare Programme in Kerala is mainly due to high literacy rate among
women. The Committee, therefore, also feels that besides, taking steps for terminal Spacing
Methods and Sterilisation methods. Efforts should also be taken for improving girls
education and for this purpose the convergence of some of the programmes in the
Department of Education and Woman and Child Education may be done.

1.5 Further elaborating on the Programme, the Secretary informed the Committee that the
health of mother and the health of child should become the focal point of the whole
programme. He further stated that if women are empowered to take decisions, then
automatically every family would be having a small family.

1.6 The Total 8th Plan Outlay for the department is Rs. 6500 crores. The outlay in first
year of the 8th Plan period i.e. 1992-93 was Rs. 900 crores while the actual expenditure was
Rs. 1090.40 crores. In 1993-94 the outlay was Rs. 1060 crores while the actual expenditure
amounted to Rs. 1312.62 crores. In 1994-95 the outlay was Rs. 1280 crores while the actual
expenditure was Rs. 1521.85 crores. In the fourth year of the plan period i.e. 1995-96 the
outlay was Rs. 1440 crores, the anticipated expenditure on the programme is likely to be
around Rs. 1768.67 crores, the Committee noted.

1.7 The Committee notes that the allocation to the department, has been reduced from
Rs. 1593.51 crores in B.E. 1995-96 to Rs. 1550 crores during the current year. Out of
Rs. 1550 crores, Rs. 1535 crores, forms plan component and Rs. 15 crores as non-plan
component.

1.8 Commenting about the allocation to the Family Welfare Programme, the Secretary
informed the Committee that the allocation from the Central Governemnt is not to the
extent desired, if we have to maintain the momentum of the whole programme. The
Secretary also informed that the Family Welfare Programme are centrally sponsored
programmes whereas the implementation of it lies with the States.

1.9 Pleading for more funds, the Secretary informed the Committee that a new
Programme named Reproductive Child Health Programme (RCH) which is the new buzz
word for family planning is being started with the assistance from World Bank to the tune of
300 million dollars and it is a client oriented programme and it is likely to be initiated by the
end of this year or in the beginning of next year. He further informed that the European
Commission has also offered 200 million dollars for the programme due to the change of
policy and change of strategy in implementing the programme.

1.10 The department further stated that the Family Welfare Programme is constantly
underfunded over the years which has led to accumulation of arrears payable to the state
Governemts. For the year 1996-97, an Annual Plan of Rs. 2400.63 crores was proposed to
the Planning Commission. However, after Annual Plan discussions, an allocation of Rs.
1700.00 crores was approved for the Programme. The Committee is concerned to note that
this amount has further been reduced to Rs. 1535.00 crores with the condition that this
allocation will absorb external assistance to the level of Rs. 350.00 crores.

1.11 The Committee is constrained to note that the government instead of providing the


3

amount that should have been allocated by the Government of India is replacing it by the
foreign aid component. The Committee feels that this should not happen. The foreign aid
component should be over and above the amount i.e. suppose to have been-provided by the
Government of India. The Committee is of the view that the department does not take any
steps for starting the fresh phase of a programme well in advance before the completion of
the earlier phase. The department should take care of this aspect.

1.12 With this allocation, the department stated that it will not be able to provide funds
to the State Governments even at the level of 1995-96. The department also stated that there
will be additional financial burden on the State Governments/UTs, as arrears due to them
from the Central Governments, are already in backlog.

1.13 The Committee desire that the Planning Commission should take a realistic view of
the Family Welfare Programme keeping in view the alarming growth of population. The
Plan outlay for the department may be raised adequately at the R.E. stage.

1.14 The Committee recommended last year for setting aside at least 3% of the total
public sector outlay for family welfare plans. The department stated that the Planning
Commission has constituted three working groups including a Working Group on Population
Dynamics and Population Stabilisation for the formulation of Ninth Plan. One of the terms
of reference to the working Group is to project the financial requirement for implementation
of Family Welfare Programmes during the Ninth Plan period both plan and non-plan
requirements and Centre-State participation for the funding, the department added. The
Committee hopes that adequate funds would be made available for Family Welfare
Programme in the Ninth Plan.

LACK OF MONITORING MECHANISM

1.15 The Committee regrets to note that the schemes funded by the Central
Government are not properly and effectively implemented by the State Governments. Many
States do not take the Schemes seriously. There is no proper monitoring mechanism either
by the Central Government or by the States for the implementation. The Committee desires
that the Department should take necessary steps to plug the loopholes and to strengthen the
monitoring mechanism for effective implementation of the schemes.

1.16 The Committee feels that in view of the failure of the State in effectively
implementing the various schemes, the Centre besides strengthening the monitoring
mechanism, should also ensure its regular control over them. Too much of decentralisation is
not yielding the desired results.

ACCURACY AND AUTHENTICITY OF DATA

1.17 The Committee was informed by the Secretary that while the rate of growth of
population in the decade of 60s was 2.2 per cent and it was 2.14 in 70s, it has come down to
the level of 1.9 per cent. The. Committee is however, of the view that the system of
evaluation and data collection are very outdated and not foolproof. Different systems are
followed in different states for registering births and deaths. The Committee feels that a
uniform system of evaluating the rate of growth of population should be adopted to arrive at
reliable authentic and accurate figures. .

RURAL FAMILY WELFARE CENTRES

2. Rural Family Welfare Centres are entrusted with the responsibility of implementing
the Family Welfare Programme i.e Planning, mobilization, monitoring, administration and


4

supervision in rural areas. 5435 such centres are working at all block level PHCs and the
number has been stagnant at the same level since 1.4.1980.

2.1 The budget allocation made to these centres in 1996-97 is Rs. 160 crores which is at
the same level as compared to that of last year. The Committee is concerned to note that
the allocation made is not sufficient even to maintain the existing centres and there is no
scope for further expansion of these centres.

2.2 The Rural Family Welfare Centres which are serving the rural poor, should not
starve for funds. The Committee desires that the allocation as required may be made at RE
stage.

2.3 The Rural Family Welfare Centres used to function independently at block level in
the initial stages Later on it was merged with the Primary Health Centres. To a question, as
to why the RFWCs were merged with that of PHCs, the Secretary informed the Committee
that the Rural Family Welfare Centres were sanctioned by the Government of India during
1950's, 1960’s and 1970’s and there used to be one Family Welfare Centre for each Block.
That used to be located at the Block headquarters. After 1980, a decision was taken at the
Central level. The Planning Commission decided that instead of having one Primary Health
Centre for one lakh population, there should be one Primary Health Centre for 30,000
population. The States were asked to implement this. The Secretary further stated that while
doing so, the States felt that the Primary Health Centre would cater to only 30,000
population and each Primary Health Centre can cover all the family planning needs.
Therefore, instead of having two doctors at the block level, one for the Rural Family
Welfare Centre and the other for the Primary Health Centre, both the centres were merged
together. Instead of having one Block Health Centre, the States oxeated four or five PHCs.
In the process, the role of the primary Health Centre got merged into the network, he
added.

2.4 The Committee is constrained to note that the Primary Health Centres located all
over the country are in a very deplorable condition. There are neither doctors nor medicines
in the PHCs. Very old, out dated, equipments are available with the PHCs. In such a
situation it is bound to affect the implementation of Family Welfare Programme. The
Committee, therefore, feels that unless PHCs are strengthened, the future of Family Welfare
Programme will be jeopardised.

RURAL SUB-CENTRES

3. Rural Sub-Centres are the peripheral Health institutions available to the rural
population for the delivery of Health and Family Welfare Services. These centres have been
opened for every 5000 rural population in plain areas and 3000 population in the tribal and
hilly areas. There are at present, 1.31,900 sub-centres functioning in the country out of
which 97757, subcentres are funded by Government of India as per approved pattern and
the rest are funded under Minimum Needs Programme.

3.1 The outlay made for these centre is Rs. 190 crores in the current financial year. The
department stated that the provision is not enough to maintain even the existing sub-centres,
not to talk of further expansion.

3.2 On the question of expansion of the Centres the Secretary informed the Committee
that the most effective person in the system is the auxiliary midwife and there is a need for
having more than one auxiliary midwife in the sub-centre. The Secretary also stated that
there is a need for comprehensive programme for taking care of the mother and the child in
addition to population stabilisation, he further added that if a major programme is taken up
for increasing the number of ANMs there would be more employment for women. He also


stated their approach to the Planning Commission is to build new centres so that more
ANMs can be coopted into the programme to make the programme more successful.

3.3 As the 9th plan is under formulation, the Committee desires that the Department
should: impress upon the Planning Commission to make a substantial allocation for sub-
centres so that more centres could be opened as these centres are peripheral health
institution and they serve the people of rural and tribal area and more number of ANMs
(especially women) could be given employment which in turn will give better results.

3.4 The Committee feels that the staff strength in position in the sub-centres is way
below the actual requirements, which ultimately affects the functioning of the sub-centres.
Moreover, the staff working in the sub-centres are not provided sufficient training to enable
them to provide an efficient service. The Committee desire that the number of Para-Medical
Staff should also be increased and the training should be regularly provided to them.

URBAN FAMILY, WELFARE CENTRES/HEALTH POSTS

4. Urban Family Welfare Centres provide Family Welfare and Maternity Child Health
services in urban areas. At present 1499 centres are functioning of which 208 are run by the
Central Sector. i.e. Ministry of Railways, Defence, Labour, etc.

4.1 An allocation of Rs. 33 crores has been provided for the current financial year and
according to the department expansion will not be possible with this allocation. Therefore,
the department propose to reorganise the existing centres only.

4.2 The Committee is deeply anguished to note that state Governments are not showing
much interest in monitoring the urban family welfare centres. On this the department stated
that the states are monitoring the Urban Family Welfare Cerires with effect from 1.4.1995
and reports have been furnished by the states of Haryana, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Tamil
Nadu, Gujarat, Orissa, Rajasthan and Chandigarh and the rest of the states have not
furnished the reports inspite of repeated reminders. The Committee desires that the
Department should take up the matter at political level.

4.3 Urban revamping scheme introduced to provide imporved service delivery, out reach
services of Primary Health Care, Family Welfare Maternity Services in Urban slum areas
could not be expanded during the last year due to resource crunch.

4.4 The department stated that during 1996-97, an amount of Rs. 32.46 crores was
proposed which included Rs. 4.6 crores for expansion of urban revamping scheme. But only
an amount of Rs. 18 crores has been allocated. The department therefore stated that the
expansion of the scheme is not possible even during the current year.

4.5 The Committee is of the opinion that these centres serve the poorer sections of
society in the urban areas, and the department should initiate steps to expand the scheme
and adequate allocation may be earmarked in future.

INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION (IEC)

5. To provide full and integrated support to the community oriented services for mother
and child health and to encourage adoption of small family norm, IEC activities were re-
oriented during the 8th Plan by carrying the family welfare programme towards the
community.

5.1 The allocation to IEC activities has been raised from Rs. 34.46 crores in 8.8. 1995-
96 to Rs. 44.05 crores this year. Justifying the increase, the department stated that during
the year 1995-96, a plan allocation of Rs. 33.50 crores was provided for IEC activities. Due


RESEARCH AND EVALUATION

to launching of some new schemes such as Swasthya Mela at PHC level, Primary School
Health Check-up Scheme and Target Free Approach and Pulse Polio Programme, the’
Budget Division was requested to enhance the Budget in the RE 1995-96. Consequently, BE
1995-96 was increased from Rs. 33.50 crores to Rs. 34.15 crores in RE 1995-96.

5.2 The Committee is constrained to note that inspite of the introduction of new
schemes only Rs. 43.00 crores has been provided on the plan side even though the
Department proposed Rs. 71.30 crores. In fact, there is no budget outlay on account of four
new schemes as compared to the normal TEC. Budget provision.

5.3 The Committee is surprised to note that without any adequate Budget Provision
under IEC four new important schemes have been launched. In order to effectively
popularise the Family Welfare Programime and also to give added impetus to the new
schemes, the provision to IEC must be adequately raised. The Committee also feels that
specific steps should be taken by the department to popularise the family welfare programme
among the poor and illiterate people.

5.4 The Committee is of the view that IEC activities should be strengthened. For this
purpose, the services of school teachers can be utilised particularly during vacations.

5,5 The Committee feels that the Planning Commission has not taken a realistic view of
the programme and the need for popularising it. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the allocation as required may be provided at R.E. stage.

DAIS TRAINING '

6. The allocation to this important programme remains at the same level as that of last
year ie. Rs. 12.50 crores. The Committee, in its 8th and 20th Report had strongly
recommended for increase in the allocation to this programme, but the Committee notes
with concern that the allocation has been’ pegged at the same level.

6.1 The National Health policy aims at ensuring 100% deliveries conducted by trained
dais, by 2000 AD. The Department stated that a proposal for a specific dais training
programme has been formulated and approved for implementation and it proposes to train 6
lakh dais during the current year under the programme. The Programme consists of training
one Dai per village in all the districts of the country in a phased manner over 3 period of
three years. | fee

6.2 The programme is being reviewed: from time to time and States whose performance
are not satisfactory are being looked into by deputing officers from the Ministry for problem
sorting and for on the spot analysis, the, Department added.

6.3 The Committee feels that the ‘allocation made for Dais training is not sufficient to
achieve 100% deliveries, through trained hands by the year 2000 A.D. as stated in National
Health Policy and also to train atleast one Dai per 1000 population. There is, therefore, a
need for enhancing the allocation sufficiently.

6.4 Explaining the objective of the Dais Training Programme the Secretary. informed the
Committee that the programme aims at strengthening the various aspects of maternal and
newborn care by improving the knowledge and skill of dais.

6.5 Since the ‘Dais’ are an integral part of rural community and most of them are
involved in the task of delivery, the. Committee feels:that they should be properly trained.
Merely distributing the kits to the dais is a waste of money unless they are properly trained.

-


PB

SPECIAL SCHOOL HEALTH SCHEME FOR PRIMARY SCHOOLS

7. A sum of Rs. 19.50 crores have been allocated for reseaich and evalustien which
includes a provision of Rs. 8 crore to [CMR this year. Explaining the reason for increase in
allocation to ICMR by Rs. 50 lakhs as compared to that of last year, the Department stated
that the family welfare programme is moving towards a paradigm shift and there is a reed
for completing clinical trials and for carrying out basic research on newer contraceptives.

7.1 The Committee is of the view the research activities in the family welfare sector
should be intensified. For carrying out research activities, especially Intra-mural and extra
mural research and for conducting clinical trials to develop newer contraceptives, there is a
need for more funds. The Committee, therefore feels that a suitable increase in the
Provision to Research and Evaluation be made at a later stage.

VILLAGE HEALTH GUIDE SCHEME

8. Village Health Guide Scheme was launched with the objective of training a person
selected by the community for Primary Health Care. It is a 100% centrally sponsored
scheme.

8.1 A provision of Rs. 10 crores has been made in 8.8. 1996-97, which was the same
last year also. The Committee is constrained to note that majority of the States were not in
favour of the continuance of the Scheme: Only the States of Punjab, Maharashtra, West
Bengal, Mizoram and Tripura were in favour of its continuance

8.2 The Department stated that the scheme is not functioning satisfactorily in the
majority of the States and an expert Group was set up to consider the steps for improving
and reviewing the scheme which felt that scheme was not serving any useful purpose and
therefore needed to be scrapped. However, the Department of Health is of the opinion that
the service of the VHGs can be effectively utilised for the delivery of health care for the
rural people and the matter was discussed in the meeting of the Central Council for Health
and Family Welfare in Oct., 1995 and a decision was taken not to introduce the new Village
Health Guide Scheme and in so far as the existing Village Health Guide Scheme is
concerned, it is left to the State Governments to take a decision

8.3 The Department further stated that in pursuance of the above decision and also
keeping in view the recommendations of the expert committee formed for reviewing the
scheme, an amount of Rs. 1.00 crore has been made for the PANCHAYAT SWASTHYA
SEVA SCHEME and the details of the scheme are being worked out by the Department of
Health. Meanwhile, the VHG scheme is continuing in its present form.

8.4 The Department also stated that the Pilot Project being considered under
Department of Health called PANCHAYAT SWASTHYA SEVA SCHEME if extended to
the whole country will cost approximately Rs. 300.00 crores and is as such, untenable. The
exercise of evaluation of school health check-up and the leading role played by primary
school teachers in this is going on and it is possible that using school teachers, may, in fact
become a viable alternative to VHG Scheme.

8.5 The Committee hopes that the recommendations made by the expert Committee
would be taken into consideration while formulating an alternative to the scheme. The
Committee, however, desires that an early decision may be taken in this regard.
STERILISATION BEDS SCHEME

9. For providing facility for tubectomy operations in hospitals run by Goyernment, local
bodies and Voluntary Organisations where such cases could not be admitted due to non-
availability of beds, a maintenance grant of Rs. 3000 per bed per annum is paid to each


8

institution subject to the condition that a minimum 75/60 tubectomy operations per bed are
achieved. The grant has been revised to Rs. 4500 per bed now. At present, 2679 beds are
functioning. An allocation of Rs. two crore has been made this year.

9.1 Commenting on the ptoposal of the United Nations Family Planning Association
(UNFPA) assisted no Scalpel Vasectomy Project and on the steps taken to popularise it the
Department stated that it has been approved by the Project Implementation Committee on
13.6.1996 with a total outlay of Rs. 4.27 crores. Out of this a component of Rs. 1.61 crore
will be spent for publicity campaign and IEC activity which includes advertisement in
national and regional language dailies/through electronic media and also towards production
of IEC material at the central level. The department also stated that other methods on
regional basis will be adopted towards popularising the new method and the perception
knowledge and attitude of the acceptors as also the impact of the method will be assessed
through. an appropriate operational research technique.

9.2 The Committee feels that the Départment should take effective steps to popularise
it among the people in rural, backward and tribal areas by preparing IEC material based on
their requirements. To ensure the family planning programme, a huge success, the
Committee feels the target should be more on men and not women because the women have
no control over their bodies and it is the husband who controls his wife body and decides the
number of children. Therefore, the Committee feels that more money and effort should be
spent on performing vasectomy operations rather than tubectomy.

AREA PROJECTS

10. The Committee is. very deeply anguished to note that the allocation has gone down
considerably from Rs. 250 crores in 1995-96 to Rs. 195 crores in 1996-97. Explaining the
reasons for reduction in allocation, the Secretary stated that it was mainly due to the expiry
of a number of on-going projects and due to the time required for finalising new projects
after negotiations with donor agencies.

10.1 About the new projects proposed to be taken up during the current year the
department stated that Phase-III DANIDA assisted project in Tamil Nadu and ODA
assisted project in Orissa are being taken up and the proposed Reproductive and Child
Health Project could be started only in Jan-Feb., 1997, the Department added. Accordingly,
only nominal provisions are proposed for 1996-97 as expenditure for remaining part of the
year. These projects are being finalised in consultation with the donor agencies and could be
started only in the later part of 1996-97, the Department added.

10.2 The Committee feels that the Department should finalise the Area Projects with
the donor agencies at the earliest and the projects should be extended to the rest of the
State especially in urban slums.

INVOLVEMENT OF VOLUNTARY ORGANISATIONS

11. A provision of Rs. 13.70 crores has been made this year, for voluntary
organisations. Keeping in view the nature and magnitude of population control programme,
the Committee feels that the involvement of NGOs is very essential. The allocation made is
less and there is a need for increase in allocation.

11.1 It has also come to the notice of the Committee that there are a number of fake
NGOs working in this field, therefore, before giving any assistance, the Committee feels that
the track record of NGO’s in the field should be verified, and NGO’s with proven track
record alone should be assisted. -


9

SPECIAL SCHOOL HEALTH SCHEME FOR PRIMARY SCHOOLS

12. With the collaboration of Department of Education a new Scheme for medical check
up of children in Primary Schools for ailments like anaemia, eye problems, night blindness,
oral hygiene and skin problems etc., has been launched. The two major fall out of this
scheme are: (1) Extensive build up of awareness among children and consequently to parents
about various health needs; (2) Basic health check up for children in primary school and
setting up of an effective referral system for cases requiring further treatment.

12.1 A sum of Rs.45 crores has been provided this year for the scheme. Asked about
the response to the new scheme, the Department claimed that Reports from 221 districts out
of about 385 districts in 27 States and UTs have been received upto 8th August, 1996 and
the coverage response has been quite encouraging.

12.2 The Committee was also informed by the Department that five States namely
Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra could not take up
the scheme, the Committee feels that the Department should impress upon these five States
also to implement the scheme at the earliest.

PULSE POLIO IMMUNIZATION (PPI)

13. In order to achieve the National Health Policy goal of eradication of Poliomylitis by
the year 2000 AD a new initiative of Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) was started in 1995-96.
Under this scheme every child below 3 years of age have been given two doses of OPV
vaccine on two specified days i.e. 9th December, 1995 and 20th January, 1996 irrespective of
the status of previous Immunization. The Department claims that the PPI campaign during
1995-96 yielded notable achievements and during the Campaign over 80 million children
were immunised on each, day. This strategy required an unprecedented logistics and social
mobilisation efforts and from the current year, it has been decided to enhance the age group
of below 5 years instead of below 3 years taken during 1995-96. The strategy will be
continued for further 3-4 years, the Department added

13.1 The Department also informed the Committee that it has been decided to
implement the 2nd phase of Pulse Polio Immunization on two days i.e. on 7th December, 96
and 18th January, 1997.

13.2 The Committee was informed that cent percent target was achieved in State/UTs
of Arunchal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Haryana, Jammu and Kashmir, Kerala, Manipur,
Mizoram, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi,
Dadar and Nagar Haveli and Pondicherry. The Committee also notes that coverage in urban
areas was in general lower than in rural areas.

13.3 The Committee feels that the Department should take steps for achievement of
target of 100% in the rest of the States also. The Committee also feels that effective steps
should be taken by the Department to increase the coverage level in urban areas also.
NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY

14. The Draft National Population Policy prepared by the Swaminathan Committee, was
presented to the Parliament in June, 1994. However the final document has not yet been
finalised. The Department stated that consultation with State Governments, UTs and various
organisations on draft was complete and it is being discussed at senior levels of the
Department.

14.1 The Committee desires that the discussions should be completed at the earliest.
The Committee also desires that the Department should try to give the draft a final shape at
an early date, in view of the rapid explosion in the population.

TECHOLOGY MISSION
15. The Committee in its 8th Report suggested creation of a Technology Mission for


10

Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan which account for 40% of the
country’s population and where the progress of family welfare programme is very slow. The
Committee again in its 20th Report urged the Department with the cooperation of the
concerned State Governments to operationalise the Mission by July, 1995. However the
Department could not operationalise it due to resource constraint. The Department further
stated that it propose to implement the Mission through externally assisted project.

15.1 The Secretary informed the Committee that substantial and detailed preliminary
work on it has been done by the Department. On account of constraint of resources, the
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) adivsed the Department to implement the measures
envisaged under the project through externally assisted projects.

15.2 In view of the country’s rising population and 40% of the population being
accounted for by these States, the Committee feels there is a urgent need to implement this
mission at an early date by the Department and it should also make all out efforts to
mobilise the resources from the external agencies at the earliest.

PRE-NATAL DIAGNOSTIC TECHNIQUES (REGULATION AND PREVENTION OF
MISUSE) ACT, 1994

16. On the question of the status of enforcement of the pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques
(Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994, the Department stated that the Act came
into force with effect from 1st January, 1996 and the rules under the Act have been notified
on the same day.

16.1 The Committtee recommends that the provisions of the Act should be
implemented in its true spirits to check the instances of termination of female foeticides,
which is a very serious concern.

FREE DISTRIBUTION OF CONVENTIONAL CONTRACEPTIVES

17. The Plan allocation for Free Distribution of Conventional Contraceptives has been
slashed from Rs. 109 crores in 1995-96 to Rs. 99 crores in 1996-97. Justifying the reasons for
reduction to such an important programme, the Department stated that the plan allocation
for grant-in-aid to States/UTs for materials and supplies under the scheme has been reduced
by Rs.10 crores and also due to the fact that the targets for Family Planning methods have
been removed with effect from April, 1996 throughout the country.

17.1 The Committee has noted that IUDs and Copper Ts are freely distributed. The
Committee was given to understand that by using them women get infection. When the
Committee sought to know as to whether any survey was made on this, the Secretary
informed that no such survey was conducted. The Committee desires that a survey should be
conducted in this regard.

CHILD SURVIVAL & SAFE MOTHERHOOD PROJECT (CSSM)

18. This programme cgnsists of two components, namely child survival component and
safe motherhood component. Under the child survival component all districts are proposed
to be convered in a phased manner. The Districts covered are supplied with Drug Kit-A.
The Committee is constrained to note that very few districts have been covered under the
programme. Further, wherever the kits are sent, they reach the end users very late. The
Department should look into these issues and ensure that the programme is covered in all
the districts of the country. The Kits should also reach the end users in time.

NEW STRATEGY

19. The goal of the country is “Health for All by 2000 AD”. While certain components
of this goal are reasonably making good progress, others such as population control have not
achieved the desired success. We are far from the Net Reproductive Rate of Unity (NRR-1)


11

and the population keeps on mounting Even though this is the last year of the Eighth Plan
and the Ninth Plan is about to.commence, still, we do not seem to be really making a dent
on the issue of solving the problem. The Committee strongly feels that a well thought
strategy should be adopted and the National Population Policy should be the first attempt in
this direction.

SOCIAL MARKETING OF NIRODH

20. With a view to promote use of Nirodh for spacing, a social Marketing Programme is
being implemented. At present there are three varieties of Nirodh available under the
programme viz, New Lubricated, Deluxe and super Deluxe. A budget provision of Rs. 35
crores has been provided this year. The Secretary informed the Committee that steps are
being taken to involve Public Distribution system for selling Nirodh in order to increase its
outreach to the far flung areas of the country.

20.1 Asked about the poor quality of condoms, being supplied and the sources of
procurement of condoms and about the quality control measures that are being taken, the
Department stated that condoms required by the Department are presently procured from
the following domesitc manufacturers:

1. M/s Hindustan Latex Ltd., Thiruvananthapuram (a Central PSU)
2. M/s London Rubber Co., Madras (Pvt. Sector)

3. M/s TTK Biomed, Bombay (Pvt. Sector)

4. M/s J.K. Chemicals, Bombay (Pvt. Sector)

5. M/s Polar Latex Ltd., Calcutta (Pvt. Sector)

6. M/s Frontline Latex, Bangalore (Pvt. Sector)

20.2 The Department further stated that random samples from lots offered for sale by
manufacturers are drawn by the inspecting Officers designed by the Department and are
tested at laboratories authorised for this purpose to ensure that condoms conform to the
specifications contained in the Schedule ‘R’ of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. It also
stated that two laboratories under the Ministry of Defence located in Thiruvananthapuram
and Madras and one laboratory in the private sector located in Hyderabad are presently
authorised to test condom samples on behalf of the Department. The condoms are accepted
by the Deptt. only after getting satisfactory test reports from these laboratories.

20.3 The Committee feels that the testing mechanism should be further strengthened
and there should be regular monitoring on this. The Committee, has, however, taken note
of the reports appeared in the Newspapers stating about sub-standard quality of condoms.

REPORT 
I. INTRODUCTION 
1.1. The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instrumental and responsible 
for implementation of various programmes of national importance like family welfare, 
primary health care, prevention, control and eradication of major diseases which form the 
main plank of our development efforts. Apart from these, the Ministry also takes special 
care for preventing the spread of diseases assuming the dimension of epidemic. The 
Department of Health, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, which is 
committed to achieve the goal of health for all by the year 2000 A.D. is responsible for 
evolving broad policies for the health sector and provides financial and technical assistance · 
to State Governments in critical areas through the implementation of important health 
programmes. 
1.2. Broadly, the objectives of the Department are to undertake National Health 
Programmes, to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to 
prevent adu.Iteration of food as well as drugs, to provide primary health care at the door 
steps of the people, to take steps for better implementation of health care programmes for 
tribal and other weaker sections of the society and also to collaborate with member countries 
of United Nations and international agencies like WHO, UNICEF, etc. in matters relating 
to health promotion and development, etc. 
1.3. The Department finances a number of health programmes aimed at controlling 
Malaria, Leprosy, Blindness, AIDS, TB, Gunieawarm either on 100 per cent or on 50 per 
cent basis. The Department also finances wholly or substantially autonomous institutions 
engaged in patient care and or research such as All India Institute of Medical Sciences, 
Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research , Chandigarh, All India Institute 
of Speech and Hearing, Mysore, Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi, National 
Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bangalore etc. The Department also assists 
voluntary organisations and institutions substantially such as Indian Red Cross Society, New 
Delhi, Tuberculosis Centre, New Delhi, Lala Ram Swarup TB Hospital, Mehrauli, etc. 
1.4. The health infrastructure comprises of 2,385 Community Health Centres, 1,693 
Primary Health Centres and 1,31,900 Sub-centres. Some of the new programmes initiated 
·during the current financial year by the Department are Urban Hospital Waste 
Management, Setting up of National Illness Assistance Fund and National Blood Transfusion 
Council, Development of Public Private Partnership and Joint Sector Approach and 
Epidemiological Surveillance and Support System, etc. Pilot projects on Diabetes Control, 
Oral Health, Prevention of deafness and hearing impairment, micro nutrient, malnutrition, 
. medical rahabilitation and cardio-vascular diseases have also been initiated. 
1.5. The overall proportion of the Budget to the Health sector has not increased since 
the beginning of the first Plan. The Health Sector including Family Welfare has been getting 
only abo\tt 3 per cent of the total outlays through the successive Five-Year Plans. The 
Working Group for Health Financing set up by the Planning Commission for the 8th Five 
Year Plan had .recommended that the Health Sector allocation should not be less than 5% of 
the total outlay. The Fourth Conference of Central Council of Health and Family Welfart>. 
has recommended that the direct investment by the Government should be raised .to a 
minimum o(S per cent of the GDP and the total investment in health could go up to 10 per 
cent. The World Health Organisation (WHO) also recommended that the public health care 
expenditure should be at least 5 per cent of the GDP if equity and universal coverage is to 
be realised. However, as per the figures available, the total investment on health and family

1.8 The Committee feels that one of the important factors leading to rise in various 
diseases is the unhygienic conditions and lack of cleanliness all around in the public life. 
Conceding to this fact, the Secretary stated tha·t a Committee under the Convenorship of 
Shri M.S. Dayal, former Health Secretary, was constituted to examine this problem. The 
task of the Committee was to examine the ground situation and evolving Comprehensive · 
National Programme on Sanitation and Environmental Hygiene on the lines of a Technology 
Mission. The Committee submitted its report in July, 1995. The Department has further 
stated that the Committee of Secretaries discussed the matter and ·suggested that the . 
recommendations contained in the Dayal Committee Report pertaining to various Ministries/ 
Departments concerned with environment and sanitation may incorporate them in their 
respective 9th Plan proposals. The Committee desires that it should be given utmost priority 
in view of the deteriorating unhygienic conditions in public life. There is also an urgent need 
to educate people about civic sense and maintenance of cleanliness all around as unhygienic 
conditions are the root cause of many diseases especially the communicable disease. 
II. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS) 
2.1 The Plan aliocation provided to the CGHS had been reduced from 7 crores in 
Budget Estimates for 1995-96 to Rs. 6.07 crores in RE 1995-96 and has further been slashed 
to Rs. 6 crores in BE 1996-97. When the Department was asked to explain the reasons for 
reduction the Department have stated that the CGHS was allocated Rs. 7 crores under BE 
.1995-96 (Plan). Due to non-implementation of disputed SIU Report of CGHS allopathic 
dispensaries the new proposals of CGHS were held up and not sanctioned by Ministry of 
Finance. Further, the approval for the 100 bedded hospital at Hyderabad which was included 
in the allocation for 1995-96 could not be obtained. Due to these reasons, the provision 
made for this purpose had to be surrendered/diverted for . other programmes, the 
Department added. The Committee is constrained to note that the Department could not 
• pursue the revision of SIU Report with Ministry of Finance. Revision of SIU Report is 
urgently needed for creation of new posts and opening of new CGHS dispensaries. Presently 
only a few cities in the country are covered and the Committee desires that all major cities 
should be covered at the earliest. Moreover, with the expansion of the metro cities, the 
coverage is not even and many pockets in these cities are not covered. Therefore, more 
dispensaries are required to be opened even in the cities where CGHS coverage is already 
there. For this. the Department would require additional funds. It is, therefore, necessary . 
that the Department should pursue the matter vigorously with the Ministry of Finance for 
the revision of SIU Report so that the allocation could be enhanced at the RE stage. The 
Committee has noted that the sanctioned strength of.C.G.H.S. ~s 7318 out of which 6822 are 
in position and 495 vacant posts are there. Posts abolished which are required to be revived 
are 166 and the requirement of staff for proposed expansion in 1996-97 is 130. The 
Department proposes to set-up five Allopathic new dispensaries and five new Homoepathic 
dispensaries, and the financial requirement for the expansion is Rs. 86 lakh per annum. The 
additional funds required for the existing dispensaries is Rs. 60 lakhs. The Planning 
Commission may consider meeting the additional ·requirements. The Committee, however, 
has examined the functioning of CGHS and submitted a separate detailed report on the 
functioning of CGHS (A Summary of recommendations is enclosed-Annexure I). Therefore, 
the Committee would not like to discuss the issues relating to CGHS at length :.il this stage.

million cases every year. Local resurgence of malaria also. took place in Rajasthan, Manipur 
and Nagaland in 1994 and in Assam, Maharashtra in 1995.

(ii) National Leprosy Eradication Programme 
5.9. This programme is implemented with the aim to achieve elimination of leprosy by the 
year 2000 A.D. The Government of India have taken World Bank assistance of Rs. 302 crores 
for ensuring early detection and free Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) services to all leprosy cases.

The prevalence of leprosy has been reduced from the level of 4 million estimated cases in 1981 
to 0.54 million on record by March, 1996. The prevalence rate of leprosy was 57 per 10,000 in 
1981 which has since been reduced to 5.8 per 10,000 population by now. A total of 6.53 million

VIII. AVAILABILITY OF SPURIOUS DRUGS 
8. The Committee is disturbed to note that spurious drugs are freely available in the 
market without any check and monitoring. This has been posing a very serious problem 
resulting in grave health hazard and consequent deaths of innocent persons. The problem of 
manufacture and sale of spurious and fake drugs in man-made and it has to be curbed with a 
firm hand. The Committee is of the firm view that the matter needs to be examined at great 
length. We can't afford to be silent spectator to innocent lives being taken away by anti­
social elements fndulging in ~h e sale of spurious drugs. A comprehensive plan, the 
Committee recommends, should be prepared to check the menace of manufacture, sale and 
supply of spurious and fake drugs. There should be provision for stringent punishments 
against the persons found responsible for spurious drugs. At a time when there are already 
many diseases like AIDS, Malaria, Cancer, etc. afflicting the nation, the country cannot 
afford to have another man-made problem like the one of spurious drugs . The Committee 
also recommends that a legislation should be made to provide for rigorous punishment to 
those who indulge in manufacture, sale and supply of spurious and fake drugs.
